items.question: Bananas store starch. As a banana ripens, much of the starch is converted to sugars. A student used semi-quantitative methods to estimate the concentrations of reducing sugar and of starch in extracts of bananas at four stages of ripening. The student made glucose colour standards from a 1.0% glucose solution and distilled water. Complete the table to show how she made 10 cm³ of each standard. Describe how the student should use Benedict's reagent and the colour standards to estimate the concentration of reducing sugar in a banana extract. She estimated the starch concentration in the same way, using iodine solution and starch standards. The table shows her results. Ripe bananas also contain sucrose. Which statement explains why the Benedict's test does not detect the sucrose in the extract? Sucrose is a polysaccharide Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar, so it does not reduce the copper(II) ions in Benedict's reagent Sucrose contains fructose, which is a non-reducing sugar Sucrose is hydrolysed when it is heated with Benedict's reagent Explain the changes in the results as the banana ripens. Explain one limitation of using colour standards to estimate concentration, and suggest how the method could be improved.
items.ms: 0.4%: 4.0 (cm³ of glucose solution) and 0.6%: 4.0 (cm³ of water) 0.8%: 8.0 (cm³ of glucose solution) and 2.0 (cm³ of water) Add the same volume of Benedict's reagent to the same volume of each standard and of the extract Heat all the tubes in a (boiling) water bath / at the same temperature (above 80 °C) for the same time Compare the colour of the extract with the colours of the standards (against a white background) The concentration is that of the standard with the closest colour / lies between the two standards it falls between Credit using a colorimeter, or filtering and weighing the dried precipitate, instead of comparing colours by eye B: sucrose has no free reducing group, so it gives a negative result unless it is first hydrolysed (by boiling with acid). A: sucrose is a disaccharide. C: fructose is a reducing sugar; it is the glycosidic bond between glucose and fructose that stops sucrose reducing Benedict's reagent. D: heating with Benedict's reagent does not hydrolyse sucrose. Starch decreases (from 1.6% to 0.2%) as reducing sugar increases (from 0.2% to 1.0%) Starch is hydrolysed / glycosidic bonds are broken (by amylase) to form maltose / glucose Maltose and glucose are reducing sugars Matching colours by eye is subjective / different people judge colours differently The concentration can only be estimated to within the interval between standards (0.2%) Improvement: use a colorimeter and a calibration curve / make more standards at smaller intervals / filter, dry and weigh the precipitate

items.name: Why animals need a heart and circulation (mass transport v diffusion)
path: Unit 1 Molecules, Diet, Transport and Health

B1.6 - why many animals have a heart and circulation
items.question: Flatworms and earthworms both take in oxygen by diffusion across their body surface. Flatworms have no heart or blood circulation. Earthworms have a blood circulation in which blood is pumped by muscular 'hearts' through vessels that run close to all their cells. The diagram shows cross-sections of the two animals. Which statement describes mass transport? The bulk movement of a fluid, with all its contents moving together in one direction, down a pressure gradient The net movement of molecules from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration The movement of molecules against a concentration gradient using energy from ATP The net movement of free water molecules across a partially permeable membrane The time, t, taken for oxygen to diffuse a distance x through tissue can be estimated using the formula t = x² ÷ 2D where D is the diffusion coefficient of oxygen in tissue, 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹. Calculate the time taken for oxygen to diffuse from the body surface to the centre of the earthworm. Give your answer in minutes. Calculate how many times longer it would take oxygen to diffuse to the centre of the earthworm than to the centre of the flatworm. Using the information given and your own knowledge, explain why the earthworm needs a heart and blood circulation but the flatworm does not.
items.ms: A: in mass transport all the components of the fluid flow together, driven by a pressure difference (e.g. produced by a heart). B: this is diffusion. C: this is active transport. D: this is osmosis. x = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m (radius) and t = (3.0 × 10⁻³)² ÷ (2 × 2.0 × 10⁻⁹) = 2250 s 37.5 min 144 (times) IC1 Flatworm: thin / flat, so no cell is more than 0.25 mm from the surface: a short diffusion distance IC2 Diffusion to the centre of the flatworm takes only about 16 s, fast enough to supply oxygen for (aerobic) respiration IC3 The flatworm has a large surface area to volume ratio, so uptake across its surface meets the needs of its whole volume IC4 Earthworm: thicker / cylindrical, with a smaller surface area to volume ratio; the distance to the centre is 3.0 mm IC5 Diffusion to the centre of the earthworm would take about 38 minutes (144 times longer), too slow to meet the oxygen demand of the inner cells IC6 The hearts pump blood under pressure, so blood moves by mass transport, carrying oxygen (and glucose) quickly to all tissues IC7 Vessels / capillaries run close to every cell, so the final diffusion distance from the blood is short IC8 Blood flow carries oxygenated blood away from the body surface, maintaining a steep concentration gradient for oxygen to diffuse in IC9 The circulation also removes carbon dioxide from the inner cells to the surface
items.why: B1.6 has come up in 9 of 21 sessions, including 6-mark explanations in unfamiliar animals (frog, Jun 2025); calculating diffusion times to compare an animal with and without a circulation has never been asked.

D: the basement membrane is a thin layer beneath the endothelium with no muscle. 4.0 and 4.2 (mm) read from the graph 5.0% Elastic fibres (in the tunica media) stretch as the pressure increases, so the diameter / lumen increases The diameter increases rapidly at low pressures because the elastic fibres stretch easily At higher pressures the curve levels off because collagen fibres (in the tunica externa) resist further stretching Collagen has a high tensile strength, so the artery does not over-stretch / burst at high pressure Veins have a thin wall / thin tunica media with little smooth muscle and few elastic fibres so the vein, which is partly collapsed at low pressure, opens out easily / offers little resistance to stretching Veins have a wide lumen compared with their wall thickness The graft cannot stretch and recoil (like elastic fibres) so the peak (systolic) pressure beyond the graft is higher / the pressure fluctuates more Blood flow is less smooth / more pulsatile / falls more during (cardiac) diastole Higher pressure may damage the endothelium beyond the graft, increasing the risk of atherosclerosis An undamaged endothelium is smooth / has flattened cells, so it reduces friction as blood flows Damage to the endothelium triggers an inflammatory response / white blood cells enter the wall leading to plaque / atheroma formation (or a blood clot) that narrows or blocks the graft

Scientists investigated whether an antibody that blocks a signalling molecule released during inflammation could reduce atherosclerosis. They used two large groups of mice of a strain that develops high blood cholesterol. Both groups were fed a high-fat diet for 16 weeks. items.question: Vitamin E is an antioxidant found in nuts, seeds and vegetable oils. Two studies investigated vitamin E and heart disease. • Study 1: 80 000 healthy women were followed for 8 years. Those with the highest intake of vitamin E, mainly from vitamin E tablets, had a relative risk of CHD of 0.66 compared with those with the lowest intake. • Study 2: 9 500 people aged over 55 who already had CVD or diabetes were randomly given either vitamin E tablets or placebo tablets every day for 4.5 years. Which of these is a free radical? a molecule that donates electrons to other molecules a molecule in which all the electrons are paired a molecule containing a carbon–carbon double bond an atom or molecule with an unpaired electron Suggest reasons why the results of these two studies conflict. In study 1, people who took vitamin E may also have had other healthy lifestyle factors (e.g. not smoking, more exercise, less saturated fat), so the lower risk may not be due to vitamin E Study 1 only shows a correlation, not causation / study 2 was randomised and placebo controlled, so it tests cause People in study 2 already had CVD or diabetes / atheroma had already formed, so antioxidants may be too late to have an effect Study 2 lasted only 4.5 years, which may be too short (CVD develops slowly) The dose or form of vitamin E may have been different in the two studies Study 1 included only women / study 2 only people aged over 55 Fruit and vegetables contain many different antioxidants (e.g. vitamin C, flavonoids), not just vitamin E They contain fibre, which reduces the absorption of cholesterol They are low in saturated fat / low in energy, so help to reduce BMI / replace fatty foods in the diet Eating them is not harmful (unlike high doses of supplements) / other studies show a benefit

items.question: Energy drinks contain caffeine and other substances that may affect blood pressure. In a pilot study, 12 healthy male students aged 19 to 22 years each drank 500 cm³ of an energy drink on one day and 500 cm³ of a placebo drink on another day, in a random order. items.ms: (128 − 118) ÷ 118 × 100 8.5% D: a placebo must be identical to the treatment except for the active substances, so participants cannot tell which they had. A and C: participants would know they had not had the energy drink. B still contains caffeine. Only (young) men were studied / small sample (12) / only one volume of one drink / only a short-term effect (2 hours) was measured / no statistical test Sample: a large number of young adults (e.g. at least 100 per group) of both sexes and a range of ages, so results are repeatable and statistics can be used; none with high blood pressure or CVD at the start Groups: people who regularly drink a stated volume of energy drinks compared with people who never drink them / participants randomly allocated to drink energy drink or placebo daily Control variables: matched or recorded for age, sex, BMI, smoking, salt intake, alcohol, other caffeine (tea, coffee), exercise, family history and medication, so the study is valid Measurement: blood pressure measured with the same type of machine, at rest, at the same time of day, several readings and a mean Duration: over a long period (months or years) with regular measurements, recording the number who develop high blood pressure Analysis: compare mean blood pressure / the incidence of high blood pressure in the groups using a statistical test to see if the difference is significant; informed consent obtained

items.question: In a survey, 500 adults aged 45 to 65 rated their own risk of developing CHD in the next 10 years. items.question: Cholesterol is carried in the blood as low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) and high-density lipoproteins (HDLs). Which combination of blood concentrations is linked with the lowest risk of CVD? high LDL and high HDL high LDL and low HDL low LDL and low HDL low LDL and high HDL Each point on the graph shows the result of one clinical trial in which people took a statin or a placebo for at least 2 years. The graph shows the reduction in mean LDL concentration and the percentage reduction in major CVD events (heart attacks and strokes) in each trial. Describe the relationship shown in the graph. In a group of 2 000 people at high risk, 160 would be expected to have a major CVD event in the next 5 years without treatment. Use the line of best fit to estimate how many of these events would be prevented by a statin that lowers LDL by 1.6 mmol dm⁻³. Without treatment, many people with FH have a heart attack before the age of 50. Discuss the evidence that high blood cholesterol (total and LDL cholesterol) causes CVD, rather than only being correlated with it. Use the information in this question and your own knowledge.
items.ms: D: LDL carries cholesterol to body cells and forms atheroma; HDL carries cholesterol to the liver to be removed, so low LDL with high HDL gives the lowest risk. B gives the highest risk. A and C have one unfavourable value each. Positive correlation: the greater the reduction in LDL, the greater the reduction in CVD events The relationship is (approximately) linear / passes close to the origin About 22% reduction in CVD events for each 1 mmol dm⁻³ reduction in LDL Reduction read from the line = 35% 35% of 160 = 56 (events) Population studies show a positive correlation between blood cholesterol and CHD deaths, found consistently in many different populations Dose–response: the greater the reduction in LDL, the greater the reduction in CVD events (about 22% per mmol dm⁻³) Statin trials are randomised and placebo controlled, so lowering LDL is the main difference between the groups, which supports cause In FH, high LDL is caused by inherited alleles, not by lifestyle, yet heart attacks happen early, so high LDL itself causes CVD (it is not a confounding lifestyle factor) Mechanism: LDL deposits cholesterol under damaged endothelium, forming atheroma / plaque that narrows the arteries But: some people with high cholesterol do not develop CVD and some with low cholesterol do; CVD has many risk factors; HDL and the LDL : HDL ratio also matter; statins may have other effects

items.question: A man aged 52 has a height of 178 cm and a mass of 96.0 kg. His waist circumference is 104 cm and his hip circumference is 101 cm. items.ms: BMI = 96.0 ÷ 1.78² = 30.3 (kg m⁻²) Obese A: fat stored around the abdomen (central obesity) is more strongly linked to CHD than total mass. B: BMI, not waist-to-hip ratio, uses height. C: neither indicator measures muscle; BMI cannot tell muscle from fat. D: waist and hips must be measured. Target mass = 25.0 × 1.78² = 79.2 kg 16.8 kg Eat less saturated fat / cholesterol, so less LDL in the blood, so less atheroma forms Eat less salt, so lower blood pressure, so less damage to the endothelium Eat more fruit and vegetables (antioxidants), which reduce free radicals, so less damage to the endothelium Eat more fibre, which reduces the absorption of cholesterol

items.question: Statins are drugs that are used to reduce the risk of CVD. How do statins reduce the concentration of cholesterol in the blood? by binding to cholesterol in the gut so that less is absorbed by preventing platelets from releasing thromboplastin by inhibiting an enzyme in the liver that is needed to make cholesterol by increasing the loss of salt in the urine Some people stop taking statins because they report side effects such as muscle pain. In a trial, 60 people who had stopped taking statins because of side effects each took part for 12 months. For 4 of the months they took statin tablets, for 4 months they took placebo tablets and for 4 months they took no tablets. The order of the months was random. The participants and the scientists did not know which months were statin months and which were placebo months. Each day, the participants scored their symptoms from 0 (no symptoms) to 100 (worst imaginable). The graph shows the mean symptom score for each type of month. The error bars show 95% confidence intervals. Calculate the percentage of the increase in symptom score in the statin months, compared with the months with no tablets, that also happened in the placebo months. Explain why doctors prescribe statins to people with a high risk of CVD, even though statins can have side effects. items.ms: C: statins inhibit an enzyme (HMG-CoA reductase) used in cholesterol synthesis in the liver. A describes the effect of fibre. B describes a platelet inhibitor such as aspirin. D describes a type of antihypertensive (a diuretic). Increases of 8.8 (statin) and 7.5 (placebo) 85.2% They expected to have side effects (because they had had them before / had read about them) They may blame normal aches and pains (e.g. after exercise) on the tablets Recording symptoms every day makes them notice symptoms more Anxiety about taking tablets may cause symptoms The mean score for statin months is only slightly higher than for placebo months (16.4 compared with 15.1) The error bars for statin and placebo overlap, so the difference is not significant Both are higher than in months with no tablets and their error bars do not overlap with it, so taking any tablet significantly increased the symptoms So most (about 85%) of the symptoms are not caused by the statin itself But the sample is small (60) / these people may not be typical of all statin users / some individuals may still have real side effects / rare side effects (e.g. liver damage) would not be detected Statins lower the blood concentration of (LDL) cholesterol So less cholesterol is deposited in artery walls / less atheroma forms So the risk of a heart attack or stroke (which may be fatal) is reduced The benefit is greater than the risk / most side effects are mild or rare, and can be monitored (e.g. liver function tests) A: anticoagulants such as warfarin reduce the formation of thrombin and so of fibrin; the main risk is excessive bleeding. B: platelet inhibitors reduce clotting, not cholesterol. C: statins lower cholesterol, not blood pressure. D: antihypertensives lower blood pressure; they do not prevent clotting.

items.question: Insects exchange gases through a system of air-filled tubes called tracheae. The tracheae open to the air through pores called spiracles and branch into very fine tubes called tracheoles, which end next to, or inside, muscle cells. Oxygen diffuses from the air in the tracheoles into the cells. A flight muscle of a locust contains about 2.0 × 10⁵ tracheoles. Each tracheole can be modelled as a cylinder with a diameter of 0.40 µm and a length of 300 µm. Calculate the total surface area of the tracheoles in this muscle, in mm². Use the formula: surface area of a cylinder, ignoring the ends = 2πrl During flight, the muscle cells use oxygen faster. Which change would double the rate of diffusion of oxygen into a muscle cell? halving the surface area and doubling the difference in concentration doubling the diffusion distance and doubling the difference in concentration halving the diffusion distance, with the surface area and the difference in concentration unchanged halving the diffusion distance and halving the surface area At rest, the ends of the tracheoles are filled with a watery fluid. During flight, this fluid is drawn out of the tracheoles into the muscle cells. Explain how this increases the rate at which oxygen reaches the muscle cells. Large insects pump air in and out of their tracheae by contracting and relaxing muscles in their abdomen. Explain how this pumping increases the rate of gas exchange.
items.ms: one tracheole: 2 × π × 0.20 × 300 = 377 µm²; × 2.0 × 10⁵ = 7.54 × 10⁷ µm² ÷ 10⁶ = 75 mm² C (halving the diffusion distance, with the surface area and the difference in concentration unchanged) air reaches closer to the muscle cells / the ends of the tracheoles, so the diffusion distance through liquid is shorter oxygen diffuses faster through air than through water a larger surface area of the tracheole walls is in contact with air air in the tracheae is replaced with fresh air / ventilation so the oxygen concentration in the tracheae stays high (and carbon dioxide low) so a steep concentration gradient is maintained between the air in the tracheoles and the cells

items.name: Gas exchange surfaces; Fick's law; the mammalian lung
path: Unit 1 Molecules, Diet, Transport and Health

items.question: Pulmonary fibrosis is a lung disease in which scar tissue builds up in the walls of the alveoli. The walls become thicker and less elastic, and some alveoli are destroyed. Which feature of the lungs maintains a steep concentration gradient of oxygen between the air in the alveoli and the blood? There are millions of alveoli in each lung. The alveolar walls are made of squamous epithelial cells. The capillary walls are one cell thick. Blood flows continuously through the capillaries around the alveoli. The less elastic walls mean that less air moves into and out of the alveoli with each breath. Explain how this would affect the rate of diffusion of oxygen into the blood. The table shows the total surface area of the alveoli and the mean thickness of the barrier between the air in the alveoli and the blood, in a healthy person and in a person with pulmonary fibrosis. Use Fick's law to calculate the rate of diffusion of oxygen in the lungs of the person with pulmonary fibrosis as a percentage of the rate in the healthy person. Assume that the difference in oxygen concentration across the barrier is the same in both people. The graph shows the partial pressure of oxygen in the blood as it passes through an alveolar capillary, in the healthy person and in the person with pulmonary fibrosis. The partial pressure of oxygen in the alveolar air is 13.3 kPa. At rest, blood spends 0.75 s in an alveolar capillary. During exercise, the blood flows faster and spends only 0.25 s in the capillary. Using the graph, calculate the percentage decrease in the partial pressure of oxygen in the blood leaving the capillary of the person with pulmonary fibrosis during exercise, compared with at rest. Using the graph and the information in this question, explain why a person with pulmonary fibrosis becomes breathless during exercise but not at rest.
items.ms: D (Blood flows continuously through the capillaries around the alveoli.) less fresh air reaches the alveoli / less ventilation, so the oxygen concentration (partial pressure) in the alveoli is lower so the concentration gradient between the alveolar air and the blood is smaller so the rate of diffusion of oxygen (into the blood) is slower rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × difference in concentration) ÷ thickness of surface 70 ÷ 0.6 = 116.7 and 45 ÷ 1.5 = 30 / surface area ratio 0.643 × thickness ratio 0.4 25.7 % 12.5 kPa at rest and 9.6 kPa during exercise (12.5 − 9.6) ÷ 12.5 × 100 = 23.2 % IC1 At rest the blood of the person with fibrosis leaves the capillary at about 12.5 kPa, close to the alveolar value (13.3 kPa), so the blood is almost fully oxygenated IC2 During exercise the blood spends only 0.25 s in the capillary, so it leaves at only about 9.6 kPa compared with 12.9 kPa in the healthy person IC3 In the healthy person the blood reaches (almost) 13.3 kPa within 0.25 s, so faster blood flow does not reduce oxygen uptake IC4 The thicker barrier (1.5 µm compared with 0.6 µm) gives a longer diffusion distance, so oxygen diffuses more slowly IC5 The smaller surface area (45 m² compared with 70 m²) also slows diffusion; by Fick's law the rate is only about a quarter (26%) of the healthy rate IC6 Less elastic walls reduce ventilation, so the concentration gradient is smaller IC7 So less oxygen is carried by haemoglobin to the muscles, which need more oxygen for (aerobic) respiration during exercise IC8 Breathlessness (faster, deeper breathing) is an attempt to increase ventilation and so the concentration gradient
items.why: B2.1 came up in 17 of 21 sessions, mostly as lung adaptations and naming Fick's law; spec 2.1(ii) says the rate 'can be calculated using Fick's law', but no paper has asked for that calculation, or used the time blood spends in the capillary.

path: Unit 1 Molecules, Diet, Transport and Health

items.question: In 1970, scientists fused a mouse cell with a human cell to form a single hybrid cell. Before fusion, the proteins in the cell surface membrane of the mouse cell were labelled with a green fluorescent marker and those of the human cell with a red fluorescent marker. The diagram shows the results. In the fluid mosaic model of membrane structure, what does the word 'mosaic' refer to? cholesterol molecules found between the fatty acid tails carbohydrate chains attached to the outer surface of the membrane phospholipid molecules moving within each layer protein molecules scattered through the phospholipid bilayer The scientists recorded the percentage of hybrid cells in which the two types of protein were completely mixed, at three temperatures. The graph shows the results. Describe the effect of temperature on the mixing of the membrane proteins. Explain the effect of temperature on the mixing of the membrane proteins. The experiment at 37 °C was repeated twice more: once with a substance that stops ATP production, and once with a substance that stops protein synthesis. Both gave the same results as the original experiment. Deduce what these two results show about how the proteins became mixed. In the Davson–Danielli model of membrane structure, a phospholipid bilayer is coated on both sides by a continuous layer of protein. Explain how the results of this experiment support the fluid mosaic model rather than the Davson–Danielli model.
items.ms: D (protein molecules scattered through the phospholipid bilayer) the higher the temperature, the faster the proteins mix / the greater the percentage of cells with mixed proteins at 15 °C there is (almost) no mixing: only 4% after 40 minutes quoted comparison, e.g. after 40 minutes 93% at 37 °C compared with 60% at 21 °C / at 37 °C the percentage levels off after about 30 minutes a higher temperature gives the phospholipids more kinetic energy interactions between the fatty acid tails break / the phospholipids are less tightly packed so the membrane is more fluid / the phospholipids move more so the proteins can move (diffuse) sideways through the bilayer and mix at 15 °C the phospholipids are packed closely, so the proteins can hardly move ATP inhibitor: the proteins move passively / by diffusion, not by a process that needs energy from ATP protein synthesis inhibitor: the mixing is not caused by new proteins being made and added to the membrane / the original proteins moved the proteins from each cell moved and became evenly mixed / were not fixed in place in the fluid mosaic model, proteins are embedded in (or span) a fluid phospholipid bilayer, so they can move sideways in the Davson–Danielli model the proteins form fixed, continuous layers outside the bilayer, so separate mouse and human proteins would not be expected to move and mix the effect of temperature shows that protein movement depends on the fluidity of the phospholipids, so the proteins must be within a fluid bilayer

items.question: The osmotic fragility test is used to diagnose some disorders of red blood cells. Samples of red blood cells are placed in sodium chloride solutions of different concentrations, and the percentage of cells that burst is measured. In hereditary spherocytosis, the red blood cells are spheres rather than biconcave discs. The graph shows the results of the test for a healthy person and for a person with hereditary spherocytosis. Blood plasma has the same water potential as a 0.9 g per 100 cm³ sodium chloride solution. Which statement describes osmosis? the net movement of free water molecules from a solution with a higher water potential to a solution with a lower water potential, through a partially permeable membrane the net movement of free water molecules from a solution with a lower water potential to a solution with a higher water potential, through a partially permeable membrane the net movement of solute molecules from a solution with a lower solute concentration to a solution with a higher solute concentration, through a partially permeable membrane the movement of water molecules through a partially permeable membrane using energy from ATP Explain, in terms of free water molecules, why a 0.9 g per 100 cm³ sodium chloride solution has a lower water potential than pure water. Using the graph, give the sodium chloride concentration at which 50% of the red blood cells from the person with hereditary spherocytosis burst. Using the graph and your own knowledge, explain the results for both people.
items.ms: A (the net movement of free water molecules from a solution with a higher water potential to a solution with a lower water potential, through a partially permeable membrane) water molecules are dipolar / have a slightly negative oxygen and slightly positive hydrogens water molecules are attracted to (cluster around) the sodium and chloride ions these water molecules are not free to move, so there are fewer free water molecules than in pure water 0.56 g per 100 cm³ IC1 In 0.9 g per 100 cm³ the solution has the same water potential as the cytoplasm, so there is no net movement of water by osmosis and no cells burst IC2 In more dilute solutions the solution has a higher water potential than the cytoplasm of the red blood cells IC3 so water enters the cells by osmosis through the partially permeable cell surface membrane IC4 Red blood cells have no cell wall, so the cells swell until the membrane breaks / they burst IC5 The lower the sodium chloride concentration, the steeper the water potential gradient, so more water enters and more cells burst; (almost) all cells burst at or below 0.30 (healthy) and 0.40 (spherocytosis) g per 100 cm³ IC6 Cells do not all burst at the same concentration because they differ, e.g. in age, size, solute concentration or membrane strength IC7 Spherocytosis cells burst at higher concentrations: 50% burst at 0.56 compared with 0.42 g per 100 cm³ IC8 A biconcave disc has a larger surface area to volume ratio, so it can take in water and swell towards a sphere before the membrane is stretched; spheres already have the smallest surface area for their volume, so less water has to enter before they burst

The amount of DNA at each density was measured by its absorbance of ultraviolet light. DNA containing only ¹⁴N has a density of 1.710 g cm⁻³ and DNA containing only ¹⁵N has a density of 1.724 g cm⁻³. The graph shows the results. Which bonds are formed by DNA polymerase during DNA replication? glycosidic bonds between sugars hydrogen bonds between complementary bases phosphodiester bonds between nucleotides peptide bonds between amino acids Explain why DNA made by bacteria in the ¹⁵NH₄Cl medium is denser than DNA made in the ¹⁴NH₄Cl medium. Explain how the results after one generation show that DNA replication is not conservative. Dispersive replication would also produce a single peak at 1.717 g cm⁻³ after one generation. Explain how the results after two generations support semi-conservative replication and refute dispersive replication. Calculate the percentage of DNA molecules that would still contain any ¹⁴N after four generations in the ¹⁵NH₄Cl medium, if replication is semi-conservative. The scientists heated a sample of the DNA from generation 1 to 100 °C. This separates the two strands of each DNA molecule. They then centrifuged the single strands in caesium chloride solution. path: Unit 1 Molecules, Diet, Transport and Health

B2.11 - the nature of the genetic code (triplet code,
items.question: DNA normally contains four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G). Scientists have produced bacteria whose DNA also contains a pair of artificial bases, X and Y. Base X pairs only with base Y. The bacteria can transcribe and translate genes that contain these bases, and their codons are still three bases long. How many different codons of three bases could be made from the six bases A, T, C, G, X and Y? 18 36 64 216 Explain why a code with codons of two bases would be enough for the 20 amino acids used in protein synthesis if six bases were available, but is not enough with only the four natural bases. In bacteria with only the natural bases, glycine is coded for by four mRNA codons: GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG. Tryptophan is coded for by one mRNA codon: UGG. UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons. A substitution mutation replaces one base with a different base. Each of the three bases in a codon could be replaced by any one of the other three natural bases, so nine different substitutions are possible in each codon. Calculate the percentage of the nine possible substitutions in the codon GGU that would still give a codon for glycine. Give your answer to three significant figures. Explain why a substitution in the codon for tryptophan is more likely to change the protein than a substitution in the codon GGU for glycine.
items.ms: D (6 × 6 × 6 = 6³ = 216) four bases give only 4² = 16 different two-base codons, fewer than the 20 amino acids six bases give 6² = 36 two-base codons, more than 20, so every amino acid (and a stop codon) could have its own codon 3 substitutions (GGC, GGA, GGG) out of 9 33.3 % tryptophan has only one codon, so every substitution in UGG gives a codon for a different amino acid or a stop codon (UAG / UGA) glycine has four codons / the code is degenerate, so a substitution in the third base of GGU still codes for glycine and the primary structure is unchanged a different amino acid has a different R group, which may change the bonds and the 3D (tertiary) structure of the protein; a stop codon gives a shorter polypeptide

items.question: In the 1960s, scientists began to work out the genetic code. They made artificial mRNA molecules with repeating base sequences and added each one to a mixture containing ribosomes, tRNA molecules, amino acids, ATP and enzymes from bacteria. They then identified the amino acids in the polypeptides that were made. The table shows some of their results. AAAAAAAAAAAA… TTTTTTTTTTTT… UUUUUUUUUUUU… GGGGGGGGGGGG… The table shows the mRNA codons for some amino acids. The scientists also made an artificial mRNA with the repeating sequence UAUC: UAUCUAUCUAUCUAUCUAUCUAUC… Deduce the sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide that was made, and explain why the same polypeptide is made whichever base translation starts at.
items.ms: A (the template strand is complementary to the mRNA: adenine on the template pairs with uracil) each polypeptide contains only one type of amino acid, so the same three bases / codon must be read again and again the mRNA is read in separate groups of three bases: UUC UUC… (Phe), UCU UCU… (Ser) or CUU CUU… (Leu) three polypeptides are made because translation can start at the first, second or third base (three reading frames) if the code overlapped, each base would be read in more than one codon (UUC, UCU, CUU…), so one polypeptide containing Phe, Ser and Leu would be made a two-base code would read UU CU UC… and give one polypeptide containing three different amino acids degenerate means that an amino acid can be coded for by more than one codon / triplet phenylalanine is coded for by UUU (mRNA 1) and by UUC (mRNA 3) / leucine is coded for by CUC (mRNA 2) and by CUU (mRNA 3) UAU CUA UCU AUC codes for Tyr–Leu–Ser–Ile this sequence of four amino acids repeats: Tyr–Leu–Ser–Ile–Tyr–Leu–Ser–Ile… four is not a multiple of three, so every reading frame passes through all four codons in the same order / starting at another base gives the same repeating sequence, beginning at a different amino acid

items.question: During DNA replication, DNA polymerase sometimes adds a nucleotide with a base that is not complementary to the base on the template strand. Scientists measured the mutation rate in two strains of the bacterium Escherichia coli: • strain N has normal DNA polymerase • strain P has a DNA polymerase that cannot proofread. The chromosome of E. coli contains 4.6 × 10⁶ base pairs. The table shows their results. What is the mean number of new mutations in the chromosome of one strain P bacterium in each generation? 0.046 0.46 4.6 46 Calculate how many times greater the mutation rate is in strain P than in strain N. items.question: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a genetic disorder caused by a recessive allele. A couple who are both carriers of this allele are expecting a baby. They are offered a prenatal test. The diagram shows two procedures, P and Q, that can be used to collect cells for prenatal testing. Which of these identifies procedure P and the cells it collects? amniocentesis: fetal cells from the amniotic fluid amniocentesis: cells from the placenta chorionic villus sampling: fetal cells from the amniotic fluid chorionic villus sampling: cells from the placenta Describe how the cells collected by procedure Q are used to find out whether the fetus has SMA. Calculate how many fewer miscarriages would have been expected if these women had had amniocentesis instead. Give your answer as a whole number. Only a blood sample from the mother's arm is needed. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using NIPT rather than chorionic villus sampling to test this couple's fetus for SMA.
items.ms: A (in P a needle passes through the abdominal wall and the wall of the uterus into the amniotic sac to remove amniotic fluid containing fetal cells) DNA is extracted from the cells (of the chorionic villi / placenta), which have the same genotype as the fetus the DNA is tested / analysed for the presence of the recessive allele (mutation) the fetus has SMA if both alleles are the recessive allele (homozygous recessive) 1850 × 0.6 ÷ 100 = 11.1 and 1850 × 0.3 ÷ 100 = 5.55 / 1850 × (0.6 − 0.3) ÷ 100 = 5.55 6 chorionic villus sampling is carried out earlier in pregnancy (11–14 weeks rather than 15–20 weeks) so the result is known earlier, giving more time to make an informed decision / to prepare if they decide to end the pregnancy, a termination earlier in pregnancy is safer / less distressing advantage: no needle or tube enters the uterus, so there is no extra risk of miscarriage advantage: it can be carried out earlier in pregnancy / it is a simpler procedure with less discomfort disadvantage: the mother is a carrier, so her own DNA in the plasma contains the recessive allele, which makes it difficult to tell whether the fetus has the allele disadvantage: only small amounts of fetal DNA are present, so the result may be less accurate (false positive or false negative) disadvantage: a positive result may need to be confirmed by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis, so the risk of miscarriage is not always avoided

Vacuole volumes: 0.40 × 2.4 × 10⁵ = 9.6 × 10⁴ (µm³) and 0.92 × 3.6 × 10⁷ = 3.3 × 10⁷ (µm³) 345 (times) Most of the increase in cell volume is due to the vacuole getting larger / the vacuole occupies 92% of the mature cell Solutes (such as sugars and ions) are moved into the vacuole across the tonoplast, so water enters the vacuole by osmosis The enlarging vacuole presses against the cell wall, so the wall stretches and new cellulose (microfibrils) is added to it The volume of cytoplasm also increases (20 times), so more proteins / organelles / cell membrane are synthesised The polypeptide is synthesised on ribosomes on the rER and enters the rER, where it is folded / transported It is carried in vesicles (that bud off the rER) to the Golgi apparatus The Golgi apparatus modifies (e.g. adds carbohydrate to) the protein and packages it into (secretory) vesicles The vesicles move to and fuse with the cell surface membrane, releasing the enzyme by exocytosis The middle lamella (calcium pectate) holds adjacent cells together / sticks the walls of neighbouring cells together so the cells separate / slide past each other and the tissue is less rigid / less firm The cell walls are weakened, so cells collapse when pressed

items.question: Mendel studied round and wrinkled seeds of pea plants. Wrinkled seeds lack an active form of starch-branching enzyme, the enzyme that forms the 1,6 glycosidic bonds in amylopectin. Similarity: both are polysaccharides / polymers of glucose (joined by glycosidic bonds) / both contain 1,4 glycosidic bonds Amylopectin is made of α-glucose whereas cellulose is made of β-glucose Amylopectin has 1,4 and 1,6 glycosidic bonds / is branched whereas cellulose has only 1,4 bonds / is unbranched Amylopectin is coiled / compact whereas cellulose chains are straight and held together by hydrogen bonds (in microfibrils) Less amylopectin / less starch is made (31% compared with 48% of dry mass) because the starch-branching enzyme is not active so sucrose (or glucose from sucrose) is not converted into starch and accumulates Round seeds have more amylopectin (67% compared with 30%), which is branched, so there are more ends at which (amylase) enzymes can hydrolyse glycosidic bonds Alternate β-glucose molecules are inverted, so cellulose chains are straight / have OH groups projecting on both sides Hydrogen bonds form between OH groups of adjacent, parallel cellulose chains Many hydrogen bonds hold many (60–70) chains together in a bundle (microfibril), giving high tensile strength

The microfibril angle (θ) is the angle between the microfibrils and the long axis of the fibre, as shown in the diagram. The table shows information about fibres from four plants. Ramie and flax are used to make strong textiles and to reinforce plastic panels in car doors, where the material must not stretch. Using the information given and your own knowledge, explain how the structure of the cell walls of these fibres makes them suitable for these uses. items.ms: C: lignin is a waterproof polymer laid down in secondary thickening. A: water can pass through the gaps between cellulose microfibrils. B: chitin is found in the walls of fungi, not plants. D: pectin (calcium pectate) holds cells together in the middle lamella and is not waterproof. 0.93 : 1 As the microfibril angle increases, the tensile strength decreases (from 870 MPa at 7° to 175 MPa at 45°) / negative correlation As the microfibril angle increases, the extension at break increases (from 2.4% to 24%) / positive correlation IC1 Ramie and flax have a high cellulose content (83% and 71%), so there are many cellulose molecules held together by many hydrogen bonds in microfibrils IC2 giving a high tensile strength (870 MPa and 790 MPa), so they resist breaking under tension in textiles / panels IC3 A small microfibril angle (7°, 10°) means the microfibrils run almost parallel to the long axis, so the pulling force is taken along the cellulose chains and the fibre hardly stretches (2.4–2.7%) IC4 Coir has a large microfibril angle (45°), so the helix of microfibrils can straighten / extend like a spring when pulled, giving a large extension at break (24%) IC5 so a coir rope can stretch to absorb sudden forces (from waves / a moving boat) without snapping, although its tensile strength is lower (175 MPa) because it contains less cellulose (40%) IC6 Coir has a high lignin content (43%); lignin makes the walls waterproof / impermeable, so the fibres do not take up seawater / resist decay by microorganisms, so ropes and doormats last longer IC7 Lignin / secondary thickening also makes coir stiff / rigid and hard-wearing, suitable for doormats IC8 Microfibrils are arranged in layers (at different angles) in a matrix, giving the wall strength in more than one direction Coir comes from coconut husks, a waste product / renewable resource: more coconut palms can be grown, so it will not run out / is available for future generations, whereas oil is non-renewable / finite Coir is biodegradable / broken down by decomposers, whereas nylon persists in the environment Coir is carbon neutral: the carbon dioxide released when it decomposes was taken in by photosynthesis, whereas burning or making nylon releases carbon from fossil fuels

items.question: The diagram shows a plan diagram of a transverse section through the root of a dicotyledonous plant. Which row correctly identifies the tissues labelled P and Q? P: xylem; Q: phloem P: phloem; Q: xylem P: xylem; Q: sclerenchyma P: sclerenchyma; Q: phloem Compare the arrangement of the xylem and phloem in this root with their arrangement in the stem of the same plant. items.name: Conditions required for bacterial growth
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation

B4.10 - the conditions required for bacterial growth
items.question: Containers made from the plant-based plastic PLA are broken down by bacteria in industrial composters. Scientists measured the growth rate of one species of bacterium that breaks down PLA in compost with different moisture contents, and in compost at different pH values. All other conditions were kept the same. The graphs show the results. Which of these conditions is needed for the growth of some species of bacteria but not others? a suitable temperature a supply of nutrients water oxygen Describe the effect of moisture content on the growth rate of the bacterium. Using both graphs and your own knowledge, explain the effects of moisture content and pH on the growth rate of the bacterium. In composters, the compost is turned (mixed) every few days. Without turning, the temperature in the centre of the compost can rise above 70 °C. Suggest why turning the compost increases the rate at which PLA containers are broken down.
items.ms: D: obligate anaerobes do not need oxygen (oxygen can be toxic to them), so oxygen is not needed by all bacteria. A, B and C are needed by all bacteria: for enzyme activity, as a source of energy and raw materials, and as a solvent and for hydrolysis. Growth rate increases as moisture content increases up to 55% (the optimum) Growth rate decreases as moisture content increases above 55% Correct use of figures, e.g. 8 a.u. at 20%, 82 a.u. at 55%, 14 a.u. at 80% IC1 Water is a solvent: substances must be dissolved to diffuse into the cells and for metabolic reactions to take place IC2 Water is needed for hydrolysis reactions, e.g. extracellular enzymes hydrolysing PLA into monomers that the bacteria absorb IC3 At low moisture content there is too little water, so there are fewer reactions / less hydrolysis / the cells dehydrate, so growth is slow (8 a.u. at 20%) IC4 At high moisture content, water fills the air spaces between compost particles, so less oxygen is available IC5 so there is less aerobic respiration and less ATP for growth / cell division / protein synthesis (14 a.u. at 80%) IC6 Enzymes have an optimum pH; the growth rate is highest at pH 7 (80 a.u.) IC7 Above or below the optimum, H⁺ / OH⁻ ions alter the charges on the enzyme / break ionic and hydrogen bonds, so the active site changes shape / the enzymes are denatured IC8 so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form and metabolism and growth are slower (5 a.u. at pH 4, 3 a.u. at pH 10) Turning lets air / oxygen into the compost for aerobic respiration by the bacteria Turning releases heat / stops the temperature rising above the optimum, so the bacteria's enzymes are not denatured Turning spreads the water / moisture evenly Turning brings the bacteria into contact with more PLA / nutrients

items.question: In 1785, William Withering published the results of treating 163 patients with an extract made from the leaves of foxglove plants. The patients had dropsy, a build-up of fluid in the body caused by heart failure. Today, patients with heart failure can be given digoxin, a pure compound extracted from foxglove leaves. Which was a feature of Withering's investigation? He compared the effect of the extract with the effect of a placebo He tested the extract on healthy volunteers first He increased the dose gradually and recorded the effects on each patient He used a double-blind design Suggest why Withering's patients were at greater risk of harm than patients given digoxin in a modern drug trial. Explain why 31 % of the patients given the placebo reported less breathlessness. Explain why this trial was double-blind rather than single-blind.
items.ms: C — Withering started with small doses and increased them, recording the effects (including side effects such as nausea) on each patient the amount of active ingredient (digitalis) varied between leaves / plants / extracts, so the dose given was not known accurately risk of giving a toxic dose / overdose the extract contained other compounds that could be harmful / cause side effects the extract had not been tested on cells / animals / healthy volunteers first, so its side effects were not known no safe range of doses had been established before it was given to (very ill) patients placebo effect: the patients believed they were being treated / expected to get better so they felt / reported that they were less breathless (a psychological effect) breathlessness was reported by the patients / is a subjective measure, not measured by an instrument some patients' condition may have improved naturally / due to other factors during the 12 weeks in a single-blind trial the doctors know which patients are given drug H so doctors could (unconsciously) influence the results, e.g. by treating or talking to the two groups differently / by recording the patients' answers differently a double-blind design removes bias from the doctors as well as the patients, so any difference between the groups is due to drug H

items.question: Scientists isolated three types of single-celled organism, X, Y and Z, from a hot spring. The table shows some features of these organisms. Which row shows the domain of each organism? X: Bacteria Y: Archaea Z: Eukarya X: Archaea Y: Bacteria Z: Eukarya X: Bacteria Y: Eukarya Z: Archaea X: Eukarya Y: Archaea Z: Bacteria X and Y both lack a nuclear envelope. Explain why Y is classified in a different domain from X. Use the information in the table. Until 1977, all prokaryotes were classified in one group. Carl Woese then proposed the three-domain system after comparing the base sequences of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) from many organisms. Explain why comparing the base sequences of rRNA is a good way to find the relationships between all living organisms. Woese's proposal was not accepted at first. Describe how the scientific community evaluated Woese's data before the three-domain system was accepted. Organism X has pili. What is the function of pili? Attaching to surfaces or to other cells Moving through liquids Synthesising proteins Protecting the cell from drying out
items.ms: A — X has peptidoglycan and no nuclear envelope (Bacteria); Y has no nuclear envelope but has ether lipids and histones (Archaea); Z has a nuclear envelope and 80S ribosomes (Eukarya) Y has no peptidoglycan in its cell wall, whereas X has Y has histones associated with its DNA / membrane lipids with ether bonds, whereas X does not so Y differs from bacteria in its molecules / biochemistry and shares some features with eukaryotes (Z), so it is not closely related to X all organisms have ribosomes / rRNA, so the same molecule can be compared in every organism differences in base sequence (arise by mutation and) build up over time, so organisms with fewer differences share a more recent common ancestor / are more closely related the results were published in a scientific journal / presented at conferences peer review: other scientists (experts) checked the methods, data and conclusions other scientists repeated the work / sequenced rRNA from more organisms and got similar results further evidence from other molecules (e.g. membrane lipids, other genes, proteins) supported the differences between Archaea and Bacteria the new grouping was accepted when most scientists agreed with it (consensus) A — pili attach bacteria to surfaces and to other cells (including for the transfer of DNA)
items.why: B4.14 is hot; placing organisms in domains from cell features recurs (Jun2021, Oct2021, Jan2022, Jun2025), while the critical evaluation of Woese's data (spec 4.14(ii)) was last asked in Oct2021.
keywords: Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation

items.name: Classification, the species concept, molecular evidence and the three domains
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation

items.question: Giraffes have been classified as one species, Giraffa camelopardalis, with nine subspecies. The subspecies were identified mainly from their coat patterns and from where they live in Africa. State what is meant by the term species. Scientists sequenced DNA from giraffes in eight populations, A to H. They used the differences in the DNA base sequences to produce the evolutionary tree shown in the diagram. The height of each branch point shows the percentage difference in DNA base sequence between the groups that it joins. Which population or populations are most closely related to population D? Population C only Populations A, B and C Populations E and F Populations E, F, G and H The scientists concluded that the giraffes belong to four species. Suggest which populations belong to each species. Give a reason for your answer. Not all scientists have accepted that giraffes are four species. Explain how scientists could obtain more evidence to decide whether these giraffes are four species, and how the scientific community would evaluate this evidence. Explain how classifying giraffes as four species could affect their conservation.
items.ms: a group of organisms that can interbreed / breed together to produce fertile offspring B — D shares its most recent common ancestor with the group A, B and C (branch point at 3.2 %), so it is equally closely related to all three A, B and C / D / E and F / G and H differences within each group are small (less than 1 %) but differences between the groups are large (more than 3 %) IC1 Sequence more genes / nuclear DNA as well as mitochondrial DNA, or compare amino acid sequences of proteins, using more giraffes from each population IC2 fewer differences in base sequence show a more recent common ancestor; compare the differences between the groups with the differences between other accepted species / compare phenotypes such as coat pattern and skull shape IC3 find out whether giraffes from different groups interbreed in the wild where their ranges meet / whether hybrids are found there IC4 find out whether hybrids (e.g. from zoos) are fertile; groups that cannot produce fertile offspring are separate species IC5 publish the results in a scientific journal so that they are peer reviewed: other scientists check the methods, data and conclusions IC6 other scientists repeat the sequencing / analysis with their own samples; the new classification is accepted when the evidence is reproducible and most scientists agree each species would have a smaller population than the single species had so some of the species may be classed as endangered / at risk of extinction so they would receive more (legal) protection / funding / priority for conservation zoos would need a separate captive breeding programme / stud book for each species and should not breed giraffes of different species together conserving each species keeps more of the genetic diversity of giraffes
items.why: B4.14 is hot (18 of 20 sessions); reading relatedness from a molecular tree recurs (Jan2020, Jun2025, Jan2026), and splitting one species into several, with peer review and the effect on conservation, has only been asked as a reclassification essay (Jan2020).

items.question: Vultures feed on the bodies of dead animals, including cattle. In the early 1990s, farmers in one region of South Asia began to treat sick cattle with drug Z, an anti-inflammatory drug. Drug Z stays in the tissues of cattle after they die, and it causes kidney failure in vultures. The use of drug Z for cattle was banned in 2006. The graph shows the estimated number of vultures in this region from 1990 to 2017. Calculate the percentage decrease in the number of vultures between 1990 and 2005. Explain how the use of drug Z led to the decrease in the number of vultures. A female vulture first breeds when it is about five years old and lays one egg each year. Suggest why the number of vultures increased only slowly after drug Z was banned.
items.ms: (40 − 3) ÷ 40 × 100 92.5 % vultures took in drug Z when they fed on the bodies of treated cattle many vultures feed on each body, so one treated animal could kill many vultures vultures died (from kidney failure) before they could reproduce / fewer adults survived to breed so fewer young were produced / the death rate was greater than the birth rate vultures take a long time to reach breeding age / reproduce slowly (one egg a year) very few vultures were left to breed (about 1000 in 2008) drug Z (or a similar drug) may still have been used illegally / treated carcasses remained the small population had low genetic diversity / not every egg or chick survives

items.question: An island in the Indian Ocean is 380 km from the nearest mainland. The table shows the number of species, and the number of endemic species, in four groups of organisms on the island. Which is the best description of the term biodiversity? The number of different species in a habitat The number of individuals of each species in a habitat The variety of living organisms in an area, including the variety of species and the genetic variety within each species The role of a species in its habitat Calculate the percentage of reptile species on the island that are endemic. Suggest why a much lower percentage of bird species than reptile species is endemic to the island. Explain why the loss of an endemic species from this island would reduce global biodiversity.
items.ms: C — biodiversity includes the variety of species and the genetic diversity within species 93.5 % birds can fly between the island and the mainland, whereas reptiles cannot cross 380 km of sea so island birds still interbreed with mainland populations / there is gene flow so bird populations are not reproductively isolated and do not form new species found only on the island it is found nowhere else, so the species would become extinct / be lost from the Earth

items.question: Scientists compared the butterflies in two nature reserves, P and Q. They also studied the genetic diversity of the common blue butterfly in each reserve, using one gene. The table shows their results. State what is meant by the term species richness. Calculate the number of common blue butterflies in reserve Q that were homozygous for this gene. A student concluded that reserve P has a higher biodiversity than reserve Q. Evaluate this conclusion. Use the information in the table.
items.ms: the number of (different) species in a habitat / area number of heterozygotes = 0.48 × 650 = 312 650 − 312 = 338 supports: P has a higher species richness (34 species compared with 22) does not support: the common blue butterflies in Q have a higher genetic diversity / heterozygosity index (0.48 compared with 0.21) species richness does not take into account the number of individuals of each species, so an index of diversity is needed the heterozygosity index is for only one gene in one species, so it may not show the genetic diversity of other species the reserves may differ in area / sampling effort, so the numbers of species may not be comparable

items.name: Measuring biodiversity: species richness and the heterozygosity index
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation

B4.17 - how biodiversity can be measured within a hab
items.question: The hazel dormouse is a small mammal that lives in woodland and rarely crosses open ground. In one region, farmland divides the woodland into small isolated areas, each with its own population of dormice. Scientists studied the genetic diversity of the dormice in ten of these populations, using one gene. heterozygosity index = number of heterozygotes ÷ number of individuals in the population One population contained 275 dormice and had a heterozygosity index of 0.36. How many dormice in this population were heterozygous for this gene? 36 99 176 764 Describe how the scientists could have determined the heterozygosity index for one population. The graph shows the heterozygosity index and the number of dormice for each of the ten populations. Describe the relationship shown by the graph. Explain why smaller populations of dormice have lower heterozygosity indices. Explain why a population with a low heterozygosity index is more likely to become extinct.
items.ms: B — 0.36 × 275 = 99 take DNA samples (e.g. from hair or tissue) from all the dormice / a large sample of the dormice in the population analyse the DNA to find the number of dormice with two different alleles of the gene (heterozygotes) divide the number of heterozygotes by the total number of dormice sampled positive correlation / as the number of dormice increases the heterozygosity index increases quoted data, e.g. index 0.18 for 40 dormice and 0.43 for 480 dormice the index increases more steeply at small population sizes / the increase is not proportional fewer individuals, so fewer different alleles in the population / gene pool the populations are isolated by farmland, so no new alleles come in from other populations / no gene flow dormice are more likely to mate with close relatives (inbreeding), so more offspring are homozygous alleles are more likely to be lost by chance, e.g. if the few individuals carrying them die before breeding less genetic variation / fewer different alleles in the population so fewer individuals may have alleles that allow them to survive a change in the environment / a new disease inbreeding increases the chance of harmful recessive alleles being homozygous, reducing survival or fertility
items.why: B4.17 is hot (15 of 20 sessions) and rearranging the heterozygosity index has come up in five sessions since Jan2022; how population size affects the index and the risk of extinction is a fresh angle.

path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation

B4.18 - how biodiversity can be compared in different
items.question: The index of diversity (D) of a habitat can be calculated using the formula D = N(N − 1) ÷ Σn(n − 1) A habitat contains four species, with 10 individuals of each species. What is the index of diversity (D) of this habitat? 0.23 4.00 4.33 4.44 Scientists compared the fish in two areas of a coral reef: a marine reserve where fishing is banned, and an area where fishing is allowed. Both areas contain the same six species of fish. The table shows the results for the marine reserve. Complete the table. Calculate the index of diversity (D) for the marine reserve. Give your answer to two decimal places. The index of diversity for the area where fishing is allowed was 1.85. Explain why the two areas have different values of D, even though they contain the same six species. In the fished area, groupers and snappers are caught for food. Groupers and snappers are predators of damselfish. Suggest how fishing could have caused the difference in the index of diversity.
items.ms: C — N = 40, N(N − 1) = 1560, Σn(n − 1) = 4 × 90 = 360, D = 1560 ÷ 360 = 4.33 parrotfish 25 and damselfish 30 grouper 132 and wrasse 380 N(N − 1) = 120 × 119 = 14280 and Σn(n − 1) = 2498 D = 5.72 species richness is the same, so the difference must be due to the number of individuals of each species (evenness) D takes into account the number of individuals of each species in the fished area one species (or a few species) is much more common than the others / numbers are less evenly spread, so D is lower fishing reduces the numbers of groupers and snappers so there is less predation on damselfish and the damselfish population increases / damselfish dominate damselfish may then outcompete other fish species (e.g. for food or space)
items.why: B4.18 is warm and a staple since Jun2021; working back from n(n − 1) to n (Oct2022 only) and explaining why D differs when species richness is the same are the less practised angles.

items.name: Index of diversity (D)
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation

items.question: Large areas of tropical rainforest have been cleared to plant oil palm trees. Scientists compared the dung beetles in an area of rainforest with those in an oil palm plantation. Dung beetles feed on the dung (faeces) of mammals. The index of diversity (D) can be calculated using the formula D = N(N − 1) ÷ Σn(n − 1) What does N represent in this formula? The number of different species The number of individuals of the most common species The number of samples taken The total number of individuals of all species The table shows the number of dung beetles of each species caught in the oil palm plantation. Calculate the index of diversity (D) for the oil palm plantation. Give your answer to two decimal places. The index of diversity for the rainforest was 8.12. Explain what the two values of D show about the dung beetles in the two habitats. Explain why the index of diversity gives a better comparison of the two habitats than species richness. Suggest why converting rainforest to oil palm plantation reduced the biodiversity of dung beetles.
items.ms: D — N is the total number of organisms of all species N(N − 1) = 100 × 99 = 9900 Σn(n − 1) = 3904 D = 2.54 the rainforest has a higher biodiversity of dung beetles than the plantation (8.12 compared with 2.54) the rainforest has more species and / or its individuals are spread more evenly between the species the plantation is dominated by one species (species 1: 58 of the 100 beetles) D takes into account the number of individuals of each species as well as the number of species a habitat with many species may be dominated by one or two species / some species may be very rare, which species richness does not show fewer species of mammals live in the plantation, so there are fewer types of dung / food for beetles the plantation is a monoculture with fewer plant species, so there are fewer habitats / niches less shade from the canopy, so the soil is hotter and drier and some beetle species cannot survive pesticides / herbicides used in the plantation kill beetles or the organisms they depend on species adapted to the plantation conditions increase in number and outcompete others (e.g. species 1)
items.why: Calculating D from a part-completed table has come up in six sessions since Jun2021; a land-use change (rainforest to plantation) links it to the human threats in B4.15.

items.name: Niche and adaptations (behavioural, anatomical, physiological)
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation

items.question: The common cuckoo lays its eggs in the nests of other species of bird, such as reed warblers. The reed warblers incubate the cuckoo egg and feed the cuckoo chick. A cuckoo egg hatches after about 12 days of incubation, whereas reed warbler eggs need about 14 days. What type of adaptation is the shorter incubation time of the cuckoo egg? Physiological Anatomical Behavioural Psychological Soon after hatching, the cuckoo chick pushes the reed warbler eggs out of the nest. Explain how this behaviour increases the chance of the cuckoo chick surviving. Reed warblers often push eggs that look different from their own out of the nest. Cuckoos that lay their eggs in reed warbler nests have eggs that closely resemble reed warbler eggs. Explain how natural selection could have led to these cuckoos laying eggs that resemble reed warbler eggs.
items.ms: A — the faster development of the embryo depends on processes inside the body there are no reed warbler chicks to compete with / it is the only chick in the nest so it receives all the food brought by the reed warbler parents so it grows faster / is more likely to survive until it leaves the nest there was variation in egg colour / pattern among cuckoos, due to (mutation producing) different alleles eggs that looked most like reed warbler eggs were less likely to be pushed out / were incubated so these cuckoos had more offspring that survived to reproduce and passed on the alleles for this egg colour / pattern, so the frequency of these alleles increased over many generations

items.name: Niche and adaptations (behavioural, anatomical, physiological)
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation
Topic 4 Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation
B4.19 - the concept of niche and be able to discuss e
items.question: The lesser Egyptian jerboa is a small rodent that lives in hot deserts. During the day it stays in a burrow about 50 cm below the surface. It comes out at night to feed on seeds and insects. State what is meant by the term niche. The table shows three adaptations of the jerboa. Complete the table to show the type of each adaptation. The graph shows the air temperature at the surface and the temperature in a jerboa burrow during one day in summer. The bar shows when the jerboa is active above ground. Describe how the temperature in the burrow differs from the air temperature at the surface. Explain how the jerboa's behaviour helps it to survive in the desert. Use the information in the graph. A second species of jerboa lives in the same desert. It feeds mainly on plant leaves and roots. Explain how the two species of jerboa can both survive in the same habitat.
items.ms: the role of an organism in its habitat / ecosystem / environment behavioural anatomical physiological the burrow temperature changes much less / has a smaller range (27–31 °C compared with 14–44 °C) the burrow is cooler than the air during the day (from about 09:00 to 21:00) the burrow is warmer than the air at night by staying in the burrow during the day it avoids air temperatures of up to 44 °C so it loses less water by evaporation (e.g. sweating or panting) to keep cool and its body temperature does not rise too high, so its enzymes are not denatured it is active when the air is cooler (about 14–34 °C), so it can feed while losing less water they have different niches / eat different foods (seeds and insects compared with leaves and roots) so there is little (interspecific) competition for food between them two species cannot occupy the same niche in the same habitat for long

items.name: Hardy-Weinberg; mutation and selection; reproductive isolation and speciation
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation
Topic 4 Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation
B4.20 - (i) understand how the Hardy-Weinberg equatio
items.question: Sweet vernal grass grows on the soil around an old zinc mine and in a pasture next to the mine. Zinc is toxic to most plants. Zinc tolerance in this grass is controlled by one gene with two alleles. The allele for tolerance (T) is dominant to the allele for non-tolerance (t). The Hardy-Weinberg equation is p² + 2pq + q² = 1, where p + q = 1. In a sample of 500 plants from the mine soil, 20 were not tolerant of zinc. Calculate the percentage of plants on the mine soil that were heterozygous for this gene. In the pasture, 96 % of the plants were not tolerant of zinc. Explain why the frequency of the T allele was much higher on the mine soil than in the pasture. Scientists recorded the percentage of plants that started to flower in each week of the flowering season, for the mine population and for the pasture population. The graph shows the results. Describe the differences in flowering time between the two populations. Which describes the isolation shown by these results? Geographical isolation, because the populations grow on different soils Reproductive isolation, because the populations flower at different times Reproductive isolation, because pollen from one population cannot fertilise plants of the other Geographical isolation, because a physical barrier separates the populations Explain how the difference in flowering time could lead to the formation of a new species, even though the two populations grow next to each other.
items.ms: q² = 20 ÷ 500 = 0.04 and q = 0.2 p = 1 − 0.2 = 0.8 2pq = 2 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.32 = 32 % zinc is a selection pressure on the mine soil / plants with genotype tt die or grow poorly there plants with the T allele survive and reproduce on the mine soil and pass on T, so its frequency increases in the pasture the T allele gives no advantage (tolerant plants may even grow more slowly), so it is not selected for the mine population flowers earlier (peak in week 3 compared with week 6 for the pasture) there is only a small overlap in flowering time (weeks 3 to 5) most of the mine plants have started to flower before most pasture plants start B — the populations grow next to each other but flower at different times, so they rarely cross-pollinate little cross-pollination between the populations, so little gene flow so alleles selected on the mine soil (e.g. T) are not diluted by alleles from the pasture different selection pressures / different mutations, so allele frequencies change differently in each population over many generations, genetic differences accumulate until the populations can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring
items.why: Hardy-Weinberg heterozygote calculations recur (Oct2023, Jan2025, Jan2026); reproductive isolation without a geographical barrier (flowering time) is examined only inside speciation answers and is a likely surprise.
keywords: Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation

items.name: Hardy-Weinberg; mutation and selection; reproductive isolation and speciation
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation

items.question: Deer mice living on light-coloured sand hills are hunted by owls, which find their prey by sight. Coat colour in these mice is controlled by one gene with two alleles. The allele for dark coat (D) is dominant to the allele for light coat (d). Scientists trapped mice in the sand hills in 2005 and again in 2025. The table shows their results. The Hardy-Weinberg equation is p² + 2pq + q² = 1, where p + q = 1. Calculate the frequency of the d allele in 2005. What percentage of the mice trapped in 2005 were expected to be heterozygous? 16 % 24 % 36 % 48 % Deduce whether the frequency of the d allele changed between 2005 and 2025. Use the Hardy-Weinberg equation. Explain how the frequency of the d allele could have changed in this way. Another population of deer mice lives on dark volcanic rock 400 km away, on the other side of a mountain range. Most of these mice have dark coats. Explain how the two populations could become different species.
items.ms: q² = 432 ÷ 1200 = 0.36 q = √0.36 = 0.6 D — p = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4; 2pq = 2 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 0.48 = 48 % q² = 608 ÷ 950 = 0.64, so q = 0.8 the frequency of d increased (from 0.6 to 0.8) light-coated mice are camouflaged against the light sand so they are less likely to be seen and caught by owls (predation is the selection pressure) so they are more likely to survive and reproduce and pass on the d allele to their offspring, so the frequency of d increases over generations dark-coated mice are more likely to be eaten, so fewer D alleles are passed on IC1 the mountain range causes geographical isolation, so there is no interbreeding / gene flow between the two populations IC2 mutations occur at random in each population, producing different new alleles IC3 the populations are exposed to different selection pressures, e.g. owls select for light coats on sand but dark coats on rock; differences in climate or food IC4 individuals with advantageous alleles (d on the sand, D on the rock) survive, reproduce and pass on these alleles IC5 so allele frequencies change differently in each population and genetic differences accumulate over many generations IC6 eventually the populations become reproductively isolated (e.g. different breeding seasons, courtship behaviour or incompatible gametes) and can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, so they are different species
items.why: Hardy-Weinberg calculations appear in eight sessions and 6-mark speciation or selection answers in five (Jun2022 to Oct2025); using two samples 20 years apart to show the allele frequency changing (spec 4.20(i)) has only been asked in words.

items.name: Zoos and seed banks: conservation of endangered species and genetic diversity
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation
Topic 4 Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation
B4.21 - evaluate the methods used by zoos and seed ba
items.question: Wild barley grows in dry, rocky areas of the Middle East. It is a wild relative of cultivated barley and may carry alleles for resistance to drought and to disease. A seed bank is collecting and storing seeds of wild barley. Before storage, the seeds are X-rayed. What is the reason for this? To kill fungi and bacteria on the surface of the seeds To dry the seeds so that they do not germinate To identify the alleles that each seed carries To check that each seed contains an embryo and is not damaged The scientists must decide how many plants to collect seeds from in each population. The graph shows the probability of collecting at least one copy of an allele, against the number of plants from which seeds are collected. It shows this for an allele with a frequency of 0.05 and for an allele with a frequency of 0.01 in the population. Use the graph to find the number of plants from which seeds must be collected to have a 90 % probability of collecting the allele with a frequency of 0.01. Explain why seed banks collect seeds from a large number of plants in several different populations of the same species. Samples of the stored seeds are germinated every 10 years. The table shows the results for one batch of seeds stored at −20 °C. Calculate the mean rate of decrease in germination between 20 and 40 years of storage. Suggest why the seed bank tests the germination of stored seeds every 10 years. Some scientists think that seeds collected now may not contain the alleles that wild barley will need if it is reintroduced to the wild in 50 years' time. Explain why.
items.ms: D — X-rays show whether the seed is full (has an embryo and food store) and is undamaged, so it is likely to be viable 115 plants rare alleles are only likely to be collected if many plants are sampled (about 115 plants rather than about 23 for a 90 % chance) different populations are exposed to different conditions / selection pressures, so they carry different alleles (e.g. for drought or disease resistance) this stores as much genetic diversity / as many different alleles as possible so that stored seeds can be used for reintroduction, or for breeding crop varieties with resistance some seeds may not be viable / may not germinate (91 − 72) ÷ 20 0.95 % per year to check that the seeds are still viable, because germination falls with time in storage when germination falls too low, plants can be grown from the remaining seeds to produce fresh seeds so that alleles are not lost from the collection the environment will change, e.g. the climate becomes hotter and drier, or new diseases / pathogens appear seeds in the seed bank are not exposed to these selection pressures / do not evolve wild populations undergo mutation and natural selection, so their allele frequencies change and new advantageous alleles may arise so the stored seeds may lack alleles that give an advantage in the new conditions / the reintroduced plants may not be well adapted
items.why: Seed banks have come up in nine sessions (most recently Oct2025 and Jan2026); how many plants to sample and the fact that stored seeds do not evolve are the likeliest new angles.

items.name: Zoos and seed banks: conservation of endangered species and genetic diversity
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation
