B4.21 - evaluate the methods used by zoos and seed ba
items.question: The Arabian oryx is an antelope that lives in the deserts of the Arabian Peninsula. By 1972 it was extinct in the wild because of hunting. Zoos set up a captive breeding programme that started with only nine oryx. The zoos used a stud book to manage the breeding programme. What is a stud book? A list of the number of animals of each species kept in a zoo A store of frozen sperm and eggs from captive animals A record of the parents and ancestors of each animal in the captive population A record of the diseases of each animal and how they were treated Explain how zoos could maintain the genetic diversity of the captive population. From 1982, oryx bred in zoos were released into a protected area in Oman. The graph shows the number of oryx in the wild in this area from 1982 to 2012. Calculate the percentage decrease in the number of oryx between 1996 and 2007. Suggest one human activity that could have caused this decrease. Before release, the oryx were kept for several months in a large fenced enclosure in the protected area. Suggest why. Evaluate the role of zoos in the conservation of the Arabian oryx. Use the information in the question and the graph, and your own knowledge.
items.ms: C — a stud book records the ancestry (pedigree) of every animal, so that relatedness can be worked out use the stud book to find out how closely related the animals are breed animals that are not closely related / that have different alleles, to avoid inbreeding move animals between zoos, or use frozen sperm and artificial insemination, so that animals from different populations breed use genetic (DNA) analysis to identify animals with rare alleles and include them in breeding this prevents the loss of alleles / keeps the heterozygosity index high (460 − 60) ÷ 460 × 100 87.0 % poaching / hunting / capturing oryx to sell destruction of habitat (e.g. by mining or oil exploration) / overgrazing by livestock competing for food to become used to the desert climate / temperatures to learn to find and eat the local food plants / find water to form a stable herd / social group before release so that their health could be checked and any disease treated to reduce stress, so they are less likely to wander away after release IC1 For: without the zoo breeding programme the species would be extinct; captive breeding produced enough oryx for release IC2 For: the reintroduction worked at first: the wild population grew from 10 in 1982 to 460 in 1996 (about 32 per year), so released oryx survived and reproduced in the wild IC3 Against: the programme started with only nine oryx, so genetic diversity is low; inbreeding may reduce survival / fertility / the ability to adapt to disease or environmental change IC4 Zoos reduce this by using stud books, exchanging animals between zoos and using frozen sperm / artificial insemination IC5 Against: the wild population fell by 87 % after 1996 because the cause of the original decline (hunting) was not removed, so reintroduction alone does not conserve the species IC6 Zoos also educate the public and local people (e.g. to reduce poaching), carry out research on behaviour, diet and breeding, and keep a captive population for further releases; judgement, e.g. zoos were essential but long-term success depends on protection in the wild
items.why: B4.21 is the heaviest point in the topic (7.7 % of marks, hot) and 6-mark answers on zoos recur (Oct2020, Jan2021, Oct2024); a reintroduction that succeeds and then fails gives data for both sides.

items.ms: the number of ribosomes in the treated cells decreases (from 4800 to 1200 per µm³ in 48 hours) whereas in the control it stays (about) the same / about 4800 per µm³ the number in the treated cells halves about every 24 hours / falls most quickly at the start the nucleolus produces ribosomal subunits / rRNA / ribosomes so no new ribosomes are made in the treated cells existing ribosomes are broken down (e.g. by lysosomes) / shared between daughter cells when cells divide in the control, new ribosomes are made at the same rate as old ones are lost readings 4800 and 1500 (4800 − 1500) ÷ 4800 × 100 = 68.8% A (nuclear pore) to show that the decrease in ribosomes is due to the loss of the nucleolus (and not to) the ultraviolet light itself, which might damage other structures / DNA / ribosomes / heat or kill the cell so that the only difference between the cells is whether the nucleolus is destroyed

items.question: The fungus Trichoderma reesei grows on dead plant material. Its hyphae secrete cellulase enzymes, which hydrolyse cellulose into glucose. items.question: Cells in the salivary glands of a mammal make and secrete the enzyme amylase. Salivary gland tissue was given radioactive amino acids for 3 minutes. The tissue was then washed and placed in a solution of non-radioactive amino acids. At intervals, samples were taken, and the percentage of the total radioactivity in different parts of the cells and outside the cells was measured. The graph shows the results. Where in these cells are the radioactive amino acids joined together to form amylase polypeptides? Golgi apparatus nucleolus ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum secretory vesicles Describe the changes in the percentage of radioactivity in the Golgi apparatus between 0 and 120 minutes. Calculate the mean rate at which radioactivity appeared outside the cells between 60 and 120 minutes. Give your answer in % min⁻¹. Using the information in the graph, explain the roles of the rough endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus in the secretion of amylase. Explain why the tissue was placed in non-radioactive amino acids after 3 minutes.
items.ms: C (ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum) increases to a maximum / peak of 59% at 10 minutes then decreases (to 4% at 60 minutes and) to 0% by 100 minutes readings 36% and 69% (69 − 36) ÷ 60 = 0.55 % min⁻¹ radioactivity is highest in the rER first because amylase polypeptides are made on its ribosomes and enter the rER the rER folds the polypeptide into its tertiary / 3D structure (hydrogen, ionic and disulfide bonds form) amylase is packaged into (transport) vesicles that fuse with the Golgi apparatus, so radioactivity in the Golgi rises as the rER falls (peak at 10 minutes) the Golgi apparatus modifies amylase (e.g. adds carbohydrate) the Golgi apparatus packages amylase into secretory vesicles, so radioactivity in the vesicles rises after the Golgi peak (maximum 66% at 40 minutes) secretory vesicles move to and fuse with the cell surface membrane, releasing amylase by exocytosis, so radioactivity outside the cells increases so that only the amylase made in the 3 minutes is radioactive / the movement of one batch of labelled amylase can be followed (amylase made later is not labelled)
items.why: B3.4 has come up in 14 of 20 sessions, mostly as 'describe the route'; tracer data were last used in Jun 2019 (inside and outside the cells only), so a time course through the rER, Golgi and vesicles is the likeliest data-based surprise.

items.question: Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes that carry out photosynthesis. They have no chloroplasts. Instead, the chlorophyll is found in membranes called thylakoids in the cytoplasm. Which of these contain 70S ribosomes? 1 the cytoplasm of a cyanobacterium 2 a chloroplast in a leaf cell 3 a mitochondrion in a leaf cell 4 the rough endoplasmic reticulum of a leaf cell 1 and 2 only 1 and 4 only 1, 2 and 3 only 1, 2, 3 and 4 Compare and contrast the structure of a cyanobacterium cell with the structure of a palisade mesophyll cell. items.ms: C (1, 2 and 3 only) similarity: both have a cell wall / cell surface membrane / ribosomes / DNA / chlorophyll in thylakoid membranes the cyanobacterium has no nucleus whereas the palisade cell has a nucleus (and nucleolus) the cyanobacterium has no chloroplasts / no membrane-bound organelles whereas the palisade cell has chloroplasts / mitochondria / Golgi / ER the cyanobacterium has circular DNA (and plasmids) whereas the palisade cell has linear DNA / chromosomes the cyanobacterium has 70S ribosomes whereas the palisade cell has 80S ribosomes (in the cytoplasm) the cyanobacterium cell wall is made of peptidoglycan whereas the palisade cell wall is cellulose prevents dehydration / retains water when the rock is dry helps the cells stick to the rock surface (so they are not washed away) protection from ultraviolet light / harmful chemicals / being eaten / viruses plasmids can be transferred to other cells (through pili / by conjugation) so the genes / alleles spread quickly through the population and more cells can survive high temperatures a cell may contain several copies of a plasmid, so more of the protein can be made

items.question: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a bacterium that can grow on contact lenses and cause eye infections. The diagram shows the structure of this bacterium. Which labelled structure is made of peptidoglycan? W X Y Z Suggest how structure Z helps these bacteria to cause eye infections in people who wear contact lenses. Scientists compared the attachment of three strains of P. aeruginosa to contact lenses: a normal strain, a mutant strain without pili and a mutant strain without a flagellum. items.question: Light microscopes and electron microscopes are used to study cells. The table shows some features of three types of microscope. State what is meant by the term resolution. Two small projections on the surface of a cell are 50 nm apart. Which microscopes could show them as two separate structures? SEM and TEM only TEM only light microscope only light microscope, SEM and TEM In a TEM image, the width of a lysosome is 36 mm. The actual width of the lysosome is 0.45 µm. Calculate the magnification of the image. Give your answer in standard form. In another TEM image, magnified × 120 000, the diameter of a centriole is 30 mm. Calculate the actual diameter of the centriole in nm. Give one reason why specimens are stained before they are viewed with a light microscope. A team of scientists plans three studies: • study 1: how the flagellum of a living sperm cell moves • study 2: the arrangement of the cristae inside mitochondria, which are about 20 nm apart • study 3: the three-dimensional shape of the surface of pollen grains. Using the information in the table, discuss which type of microscope would be most suitable for each study.
items.ms: the ability to distinguish between two points that are close together (as separate points) A (SEM and TEM only) 36 mm = 36000 µm / correct conversion to the same units 36000 ÷ 0.45 = 8.0 × 10⁴ 30 mm = 30 × 10⁶ nm / 3.0 × 10⁷ nm 3.0 × 10⁷ ÷ 1.2 × 10⁵ = 250 nm to increase the contrast between structures / to make transparent / colourless structures visible / to identify particular structures or molecules (e.g. chromosomes, starch) IC1 Study 1: light microscope, because it is the only one that can view living specimens / specimens for electron microscopes are dead (in a vacuum) IC2 Study 1: the flagellum (about 1 µm wide / longer than 50 µm) is larger than 200 nm, so it can be resolved and its movement watched in real time at up to × 1500 IC3 Study 1: limitation: the light microscope cannot resolve the internal structure of the flagellum (microtubules) IC4 Study 2: cristae 20 nm apart are closer than the 200 nm resolution of the light microscope, so they would not be seen as separate IC5 Study 2: TEM, because its resolution (0.5 nm) is high enough and it shows internal structures in thin sections, whereas the SEM shows only surfaces IC6 Study 3: SEM, because it gives a three-dimensional image of the surface and its resolution (10 nm) shows fine surface detail IC7 Study 3: the TEM gives only a two-dimensional section, and the light microscope's resolution is too low for fine surface features IC8 Electron microscope images are black and white and specimen preparation may cause artefacts; the light microscope can show colour with stains
items.why: Magnification from an image has come up in 12 sessions and resolution or 'why not visible with a light microscope' in most others; choosing between the light microscope, TEM and SEM was asked only as a 1-mark naming (Jan 2026), so a 6-mark discussion of microscope choice is a likely extension.

items.name: Locus and linkage of genes

items.question: In a species of flowering plant: • gene R/r controls flower colour • gene H/h controls whether the leaves are hairy • gene S/s controls seed shape • gene T/t controls stem height. Scientists found the percentage of each type of gamete produced by three plants. Each plant was heterozygous for two of these genes, and had inherited both dominant alleles from one parent and both recessive alleles from the other parent. The table shows the results. State what is meant by the term locus. Which statement about genes and alleles is correct? Alleles of the same gene are found at the same locus on homologous chromosomes. Different alleles of a gene are found at different loci on homologous chromosomes. Linked genes are found at the same locus on one chromosome. Linked genes are found on different chromosomes. Explain why plant 1 produced 4% of gametes with the alleles Rh and 4% with rH. Deduce whether genes R and S are linked. Give a reason for your answer. Calculate the percentage of recombinant gametes produced by plant 3, and use this to deduce whether the loci of H and T are closer together or further apart than the loci of R and H. Plant 4 is also heterozygous for genes R and H, but it inherited the alleles R and h from one parent and r and H from the other parent. Predict the percentage of each type of gamete that plant 4 would produce. Explain your answer.
items.ms: the position / location of a gene on a chromosome A (Alleles of the same gene are found at the same locus on homologous chromosomes.) the genes R and H are linked / on the same chromosome so the alleles R and H (and r and h) are usually inherited together Rh and rH are recombinants produced by crossing over (in prophase I) between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes / at a chiasma the loci are close together, so crossing over between them is rare not linked / on different chromosomes because all four types of gamete are produced in equal proportions (25% each), as expected from independent assortment (in metaphase I) recombinants (Ht + hT) = 15 + 15 = 30% H and T are further apart, because crossing over between them is more likely (30% compared with 8% recombinants) Rh 46% and rH 46% RH 4% and rh 4% R and h (and r and H) are now on the same chromosome so are inherited together; RH and rh are now the recombinants, formed by crossing over at the same frequency (the loci are the same distance apart)

items.ms: B (L) homologous chromosomes are separated in meiosis I / anaphase I (and two cells form) (sister) chromatids are separated in meiosis II / anaphase II (and the cells divide again) so the gametes are haploid / contain half the DNA of a body cell 92 chromatids 23 chromosomes both (homologous) chromosomes 21 move to the same pole (in anaphase I) so the egg cell has two copies of chromosome 21 / 24 chromosomes the egg is fertilised by a (normal) sperm with one chromosome 21 / 23 chromosomes the nuclei fuse, so the zygote has three copies / 47 chromosomes, which are copied (by mitosis) into all body cells 119 − 29.6 = 89.4 89.4 ÷ 29.6 × 100 = 302% the older the mother, the longer her primary oocytes have been held in prophase I / meiosis I more time for damage to / deterioration of the spindle fibres / the proteins holding the chromosomes more time for exposure to mutagens / radiation / harmful chemicals so the homologous chromosomes are more likely to fail to separate (non-disjunction in anaphase I) the frequency rises steeply after 35 (about 45 times higher at 45 than at 20)

items.name: Meiosis and genetic variation
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation

B3.10 - the role of meiosis in ensuring genetic varia
items.question: In one species of leaf-cutting ant, the queen and the workers are female. They develop from fertilised eggs, and their body cells contain 22 chromosomes. Male ants develop from eggs that are not fertilised. The diagram shows part of the life cycle of this ant. Give the number of chromosomes in an egg cell and in a body cell of a male ant. Name the stage of meiosis in which independent assortment of chromosomes takes place. Calculate the number of different combinations of chromosomes that are possible in the egg cells of a queen as a result of independent assortment alone. A male ant produces sperm cells by a type of cell division that does not halve the number of chromosomes. Which describes the sperm cells produced by one male? diploid and genetically different from each other diploid and genetically identical to each other haploid and genetically different from each other haploid and genetically identical to each other Workers that have the same mother and the same father are more genetically similar to each other than two human sisters with the same parents. Explain why. A queen of this species mates with several males and stores their sperm. Scientists compared colonies whose workers all had one father with colonies whose workers had five or more fathers. They used 12 colonies of each type. Workers from each colony were exposed to the spores of a parasitic fungus, and the percentage of workers that died within 10 days was recorded. The graph shows the results. The error bars show ± 1 standard deviation. Using the information in the graph and your knowledge of meiosis, explain why colonies whose workers have several fathers are more likely to survive infection by this fungus.
items.ms: egg cell: 11 body cell of a male: 11 metaphase I 11 homologous pairs / 2¹¹ 2048 D (haploid and genetically identical to each other) all the sperm from one male ant are genetically identical / carry the same alleles (because) the male is haploid / has no homologous pairs, so there is no crossing over or independent assortment when it makes sperm so workers with the same father all receive the same paternal alleles / chromosomes genetic differences between these workers come only from the queen's eggs (maternal chromosomes) in humans the father's sperm are genetically different (crossing over and independent assortment), so sisters inherit different paternal alleles IC1 Fewer workers died in colonies with five or more fathers (34% compared with 62%) IC2 The error bars do not overlap, so the difference is likely to be significant IC3 With one father, all workers receive the same paternal alleles (identical sperm), so the colony has low genetic diversity IC4 Different males carry different alleles (each male came from an egg produced by meiosis), so several fathers give the workers more different combinations of alleles IC5 Crossing over in prophase I of the queen's meiosis produces new combinations of alleles on her chromosomes IC6 Independent assortment in metaphase I gives different combinations of the queen's chromosomes in each egg, adding variation in both types of colony IC7 Greater genetic diversity means some workers are more likely to have alleles that give resistance to the fungus, so fewer workers die and the infection spreads less IC8 Limitations: only 12 colonies of each type / the colonies may differ in other ways (e.g. age, size, site) / only one fungus tested
items.why: B3.10 has come up in 19 of 20 sessions (4.9% of marks); life-cycle chromosome numbers (Jan 2023 liverwort) and 'explain the variation' recur, but an organism with haploid males and the 2ⁿ count of chromosome combinations have not been asked.

path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation

B3.11 - how mammalian gametes are specialised for the
items.question: Human sperm cells are specialised to swim to an egg cell and fertilise it. How many of these statements about a human sperm cell are correct? • It contains a haploid nucleus. • Its acrosome contains hydrolytic enzymes. • Its midpiece contains many mitochondria that provide ATP. • Its cytoplasm contains cortical granules. 1 2 3 4 Men with Kartagener syndrome produce sperm cells with flagella that cannot move, even though the midpiece contains normal mitochondria. Explain why these men are usually infertile. These men can have children by intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), in which one sperm cell is injected directly into the cytoplasm of an egg cell. Suggest why ICSI can be successful even though the sperm cells cannot swim.
items.ms: C (3) the sperm cells cannot swim (through the cervix, uterus and oviduct) so they cannot reach the egg cell (in the oviduct) / reach and penetrate the zona pellucida, so fertilisation does not happen the sperm does not need to swim to the egg / ICSI places it inside the egg, bypassing the zona pellucida the sperm still has a normal haploid nucleus / normal DNA so the sperm nucleus can fuse with the egg nucleus to form a diploid zygote
items.why: Sperm specialisation (flagellum, mitochondria, acrosome) has come up in most sessions (Jan 2025, Oct 2025); an infertility context in which only one feature fails has not been used.

items.name: Mammalian gametes: specialisation
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation

B3.11 - how mammalian gametes are specialised for the
items.question: The diagram shows a human egg cell surrounded by follicle cells. Which describes structure X? zona pellucida: a layer of glycoprotein that sperm cells bind to zona pellucida: a phospholipid bilayer that controls what enters the egg cell zona pellucida: a layer of glycoprotein that releases enzymes to digest sperm cells zona pellucida: a layer of follicle cells that supplies the egg cell with nutrients The cytoplasm of the egg cell contains many lipid droplets. Explain how the lipid droplets adapt the egg cell for its function. The diameter of the egg cell, not including the zona pellucida, is 110 µm. The volume of a human sperm cell is about 28 µm³. Calculate how many times greater the volume of the egg cell is than the volume of a sperm cell. Use the formula: volume of a sphere = 4/3 πr³ Give your answer in standard form. Scientists counted the number of mitochondria in egg cells collected from women having IVF treatment. Each egg cell was then fertilised, and the scientists recorded whether it developed into a healthy embryo. The graph shows the results. The number of egg cells in each group (n) is shown above each bar. Using the information in the graph and your own knowledge, discuss whether the number of mitochondria in an egg cell affects whether it develops into a healthy embryo. Explain why it is important that the nucleus of the egg cell is haploid.
items.ms: A (zona pellucida: a layer of glycoprotein that sperm cells bind to) lipids are a store of respiratory substrate / energy (hydrolysed and) respired to provide / release ATP for the zygote / early embryo (e.g. for cell division) until it implants / receives nutrients from the mother r = 55 µm volume of egg cell = 4/3 × π × 55³ = 6.97 × 10⁵ µm³ ÷ 28 = 2.5 × 10⁴ IC1 The percentage developing into a healthy embryo increases as the number of mitochondria increases, from 12% (below 100 000) to 57% (400 000 or more) IC2 The increase levels off above about 300 000 mitochondria (55% to 57%), so more mitochondria give little extra benefit IC3 Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which produces ATP IC4 ATP is needed by the zygote / early embryo for mitosis / cell division, DNA replication and protein synthesis IC5 The sperm contributes few or no mitochondria, so the early embryo depends on the mitochondria of the egg cell IC6 This is a correlation, which does not prove that the mitochondria cause the difference; other factors (e.g. age of the woman, quality of the egg or sperm) may affect both IC7 Only 25 eggs in the lowest group / no error bars or statistical test, so it is not known whether the differences are significant IC8 Even with the most mitochondria fewer than 60% developed, so other factors must also be important the egg nucleus fuses with a haploid sperm nucleus at fertilisation so the zygote is diploid / has 46 chromosomes / the chromosome number stays the same from one generation to the next

items.question: After fertilisation, the zona pellucida of a mammalian egg cell hardens. Scientists investigated this by placing mouse egg cells in a solution of a protease enzyme. They recorded the time taken for the zona pellucida to be digested completely. The table shows their results. Where are the cortical granules found in an unfertilised egg cell? in the cytoplasm, just inside the cell surface membrane in the zona pellucida in the nucleus between the cell surface membrane and the zona pellucida Explain the results shown in the table. Explain why the hardening of the zona pellucida is important for the development of a normal embryo.
items.ms: A (cortical granules are vesicles lying just beneath the cell surface membrane) after fertilisation, the cortical granules fuse with the cell surface membrane and release (their) enzymes the enzymes modify the glycoproteins of the zona pellucida / cause the zona pellucida to harden the hardened zona pellucida is more resistant to digestion by the protease, so it takes longer to digest (46.5 min compared with 2.4 min) when the cortical granules cannot fuse with the membrane, no enzymes are released, so the zona pellucida does not harden and is digested about as quickly as in an unfertilised egg cell (2.9 min) it prevents (more) sperm cells binding to / digesting through the zona pellucida / prevents polyspermy so only one (haploid) sperm nucleus fuses with the (haploid) egg nucleus so the zygote is diploid / has the correct number of chromosomes

items.name: Fertilisation in mammals: acrosome reaction, cortical reaction, fusion of nuclei
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation

B3.12 - the process of fertilisation in mammals, incl
items.question: In mice, a sperm cell undergoes the acrosome reaction when it binds to the zona pellucida of an egg cell. The zona pellucida contains three glycoproteins, ZP1, ZP2 and ZP3. Scientists incubated samples of mouse sperm cells for 30 minutes in solutions that each contained one of these glycoproteins. One sample was incubated with ZP3 from which all the carbohydrate chains had been removed. A control sample was incubated with no glycoprotein. The sperm cells were then stained to show which of them had undergone the acrosome reaction. The graph shows the results. The error bars show ± one standard deviation. Some events that take place during fertilisation in mammals are listed. 1 cortical granules fuse with the cell surface membrane of the egg cell 2 enzymes digest a path through the zona pellucida 3 the sperm cell binds to the zona pellucida 4 the sperm cell membrane fuses with the egg cell membrane Which is the correct sequence of these events? 2, 3, 1, 4 3, 2, 1, 4 3, 4, 2, 1 3, 2, 4, 1 Calculate the percentage increase in the sperm cells that had undergone the acrosome reaction when they were incubated with ZP3, compared with the control. Comment on what these results suggest about how the acrosome reaction is triggered. Some men are infertile because their sperm cells undergo the acrosome reaction before they reach an egg cell. Explain why these sperm cells are unlikely to fertilise an egg cell. The acrosome forms from vesicles produced by the Golgi apparatus of a developing sperm cell. A drug stops vesicles moving from the rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) to the Golgi apparatus. Explain why sperm cells that develop in the presence of this drug would not be able to fertilise an egg cell.
items.ms: D (the sperm binds to ZP3, the acrosome reaction digests the zona, the membranes fuse and then the cortical reaction follows) 66 − 12 = 54 / (66 − 12) ÷ 12 × 100 450 % ZP3 triggers the acrosome reaction / ZP3 gave the highest percentage (66 % compared with 12 % in the control) the error bars for ZP3 do not overlap with those for the control, so the difference is likely to be significant ZP1 and ZP2 do not trigger the acrosome reaction: their error bars overlap with the control, so there is no significant difference sperm cells have a receptor (protein) on their cell surface membrane that is complementary to (part of) ZP3 the carbohydrate chains of ZP3 are needed to bind to the receptor / to trigger the reaction, because removing them reduced the percentage to 17 % / to about the control value the (digestive) enzymes / acrosin are released (from the acrosome) before the sperm cell reaches the zona pellucida the enzymes diffuse away / are lost (in the fluid of the female reproductive tract) / are not concentrated at the zona pellucida so the sperm cell cannot digest a path through the zona pellucida (to reach the egg cell membrane) the sperm cell may no longer be able to bind to ZP3 / the zona pellucida so the sperm cell membrane cannot fuse with the egg cell membrane / the sperm nucleus cannot enter the egg cell (and fuse with the egg nucleus) the acrosome enzymes (acrosin) are proteins made on the ribosomes of the rER the enzymes cannot reach the Golgi apparatus to be modified / packaged into vesicles (that form the acrosome) so the acrosome has no (digestive) enzymes / no acrosome forms, and the zona pellucida cannot be digested
items.why: B3.12 has come up in 12 of 20 sessions and the acrosome reaction was asked in Oct2024 and Jun2025, but data on which zona glycoprotein triggers it, and the effect of a premature acrosome reaction, have never been asked.

items.question: A student investigated the effect of sucrose concentration on the growth of pollen tubes. • Pollen grains from one flower were placed in drops of sucrose solution on cavity slides. • Seven sucrose concentrations were used, from 0 % to 30 %. • After 2 hours at 25 °C, the length of 20 pollen tubes on each slide was measured using an eyepiece graticule. The graph shows the mean length of the pollen tubes at each sucrose concentration. Which nucleus controls the growth of the pollen tube? generative nucleus tube nucleus male nucleus polar nucleus The student calibrated the eyepiece graticule using a stage micrometer. 40 eyepiece graticule divisions were equal to 0.25 mm on the stage micrometer. items.question: Strawberry plants (Fragaria vesca) reproduce asexually by growing runners. A runner is a stem that grows along the ground. New plants develop where a runner touches the soil, from cells that divide by mitosis. The diploid number (2n) of this strawberry species is 14. Which describes the chromosomes in a strawberry cell at the start of metaphase of mitosis? 14 chromosomes, each made of two chromatids 7 chromosomes, each made of two chromatids 28 chromosomes, each made of one chromatid 14 chromosomes, each made of one chromatid The pie chart shows the proportion of time that a cell in the tip of a strawberry runner spends in each stage of the cell cycle. One complete cell cycle takes 18 hours. Calculate the time, in minutes, that this cell spends in metaphase. Describe what happens to the chromosomes during metaphase. Strawberry growers produce new plants from runners rather than from seeds. Explain why all the plants produced from the runners of one parent plant are genetically identical to the parent plant.
items.ms: A (2n = 14 chromosomes; DNA was replicated in interphase so each has two sister chromatids) 12 ÷ 360 × 18 (× 60) / 1° = 3 minutes 36 minutes the chromosomes (each of two chromatids) line up on the equator / in the middle of the cell each chromosome is attached to spindle fibres by its centromere the two chromatids of each chromosome are attached to spindle fibres from opposite poles the cells of the new plants are produced by mitosis (from cells of the parent) DNA is replicated (in interphase) to form two identical (sister) chromatids the chromatids are separated (in anaphase), so each daughter cell receives one copy of each chromosome there is no meiosis / no fertilisation, so no new combinations of alleles (no crossing over or independent assortment)
items.why: B3.14 is hot; pie charts of the cycle (Jun2019, Jun2022, Jan2025) were answered correctly by only about a third of candidates, metaphase has never been asked to be described, and the spec's asexual reproduction is rarely tested.

items.name: Mitosis and the cell cycle
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation
Topic 3 Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development
B3.14 - the role of mitosis and the cell cycle in pro
items.question: Scientists measured the mass of DNA in each of 10 000 cells from a culture of human cells that were dividing by mitosis. They then treated a second culture with drug V for 24 hours and measured the mass of DNA in 10 000 of its cells. Drug V prevents spindle fibres from forming. The graphs and the table show the results. Which of these cells would have a relative mass of DNA of 2.0? a cell that has just completed cytokinesis a cell that is replicating its DNA a cell in metaphase a cell in interphase that has not yet replicated its DNA Explain the distribution of the mass of DNA in the untreated cells. The cell cycle of the untreated cells lasts 22 hours. The number of cells in each group is proportional to the time each cell spends in that group. Use the information in the table to calculate the time that an untreated cell spends replicating its DNA. Explain the differences between the results for the untreated cells and the cells treated with drug V. Some of the treated cells had a relative mass of DNA of 4.0. Suggest how these cells were formed. Drugs similar to drug V are used to treat some cancers. Suggest why these drugs slow the growth of a tumour but can also cause hair loss.
items.ms: C (DNA has been replicated, so each chromosome has two chromatids until anaphase) cells with a mass of 1.0 have not (yet) replicated their DNA / have just divided / are in (early) interphase most cells have a mass of 1.0 because cells spend longest in this part of the cycle cells with a mass between 1.0 and 2.0 are replicating their DNA (during interphase) cells with a mass of 2.0 have replicated their DNA / each chromosome has two chromatids; they are in late interphase or in mitosis the mass halves (from 2.0 to 1.0) when the cell divides (at cytokinesis), giving two cells 2800 ÷ 10000 (= 0.28) × 22 6.2 hours without spindle fibres the chromosomes cannot attach (by their centromeres) / cannot line up on the equator (in metaphase) (sister) chromatids cannot be separated / pulled to opposite poles (in anaphase) so the cells cannot complete mitosis / do not divide (no cytokinesis) so cells build up with a DNA mass of 2.0 (7900 compared with 1600) fewer cells have a mass of 1.0 because no new daughter cells are produced (700 compared with 5600) cells that could not complete mitosis returned to interphase without dividing / without cytokinesis (a nuclear envelope formed around all the chromatids and) the DNA was replicated again, doubling the mass from 2.0 to 4.0 tumour cells divide (rapidly / uncontrollably) by mitosis, so the drug stops new tumour cells being produced cells in hair follicles / roots of hairs also divide rapidly by mitosis, so they are also prevented from dividing and hair is not replaced
items.why: B3.14 is hot (18 of 20 sessions); DNA-content graphs (Oct2020, Jan2022) and spindle-fibre drugs (Oct2022) recur, but the DNA content of a whole population of cells, and cells re-replicating after a failed mitosis, have not been asked.

items.question: A student prepared a root tip squash to observe the stages of mitosis in garlic (Allium sativum) roots. The diagram shows a longitudinal section through the tip of a garlic root. P, Q, R and S are four regions of the root. The student cut off the last 3 mm of the root and discarded the rest. Use the diagram to explain why only the last 3 mm of the root was used. items.name: Stem cells: totipotent, pluripotent, morula, blastocyst; society's use of stem cells
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation
Topic 3 Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development
B3.17 - (i) understand what is meant by the terms ste
items.question: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a common cause of loss of sight in older people. In AMD, a layer of cells at the back of the eye, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), is damaged. In clinical trials, patients with AMD have been given RPE cells grown from pluripotent stem cells. The diagram shows a section through a human blastocyst. Pluripotent stem cells can be obtained from a blastocyst. Which structure contains the pluripotent stem cells? W X Y Z State the differences between a pluripotent stem cell and a totipotent stem cell. Some scientists are concerned that a few undifferentiated pluripotent stem cells could be injected into the eye with the RPE cells. Suggest why this could harm the patient. RPE cells for treating AMD can be made from: • embryonic stem cells taken from spare embryos left over from IVF treatment • induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells), made by changing the gene expression of skin cells taken from the patient. Discuss how society might decide whether RPE cells made from each type of stem cell should be used to treat patients with AMD.
items.ms: C (Y is the inner cell mass) totipotent stem cells can differentiate into any type of cell, including extra-embryonic / placenta cells pluripotent stem cells can differentiate into most types of cell but not extra-embryonic / placenta cells totipotent cells are found in the morula / very early embryo, whereas pluripotent cells are found in the inner cell mass of the blastocyst pluripotent stem cells can continue to divide by mitosis (uncontrollably) / could form a tumour they could differentiate into other (unwanted) types of cell / tissue in the eye this could damage the retina / block light / make sight worse IC1 Embryonic stem cells: obtaining them destroys the embryo / blastocyst; some people believe an embryo is a potential human with a right to life (religious / ethical objection) IC2 Embryonic stem cells: the embryos are spare IVF embryos that would otherwise be destroyed; at about 5 days the embryo has no nervous system and cannot feel pain; the IVF patients must give informed consent IC3 iPS cells: no embryo is destroyed, so there are fewer ethical objections; the cells come from the patient, who can consent; they are genetically identical to the patient's cells so are less likely to be rejected IC4 iPS cells: changing gene expression may make the cells less safe / more likely to form tumours / they may not behave exactly like embryonic stem cells; making cells for each patient is slow and expensive IC5 Both: risk of tumours or unwanted cell types must be weighed against the benefit; AMD is common and causes blindness, so many people could regain sight / improve their quality of life IC6 Decision: based on scientific evidence that has been peer reviewed and from clinical trials (safety first tested on small numbers of patients); made by regulatory authorities / ethics committees that license the use, taking account of public opinion and religious and cultural views; laws differ between countries
items.why: B3.17 has come up in 14 of 20 sessions; society's decisions about stem cells have been asked only as short 'suggest why approved' parts (Oct2022, Jun2025), so a 6-mark discussion comparing embryonic and induced pluripotent stem cells is the likeliest surprise.

items.name: Differential gene expression and cell specialisation
path: Unit 2 Cells, Development, Biodiversity and Conservation

items.question: Use the information in the scientific article and your own knowledge to answer the questions that follow. Brown fat: the tissue that burns fuel to make heat (1) Most fat in the human body is stored in white adipose tissue. Each white fat cell contains one large droplet of triglyceride and few mitochondria. Brown adipose tissue, or brown fat, is different. Its cells contain many small lipid droplets and very large numbers of mitochondria. These mitochondria are rich in cytochromes, the iron-containing electron carriers that give the tissue its colour. About 5% of the body mass of a newborn baby is brown fat, most of it between the shoulder blades. (2) In most cells, the electron transport chain and ATP synthase are tightly coupled: protons pumped into the intermembrane space can return to the matrix only through ATP synthase. The inner mitochondrial membrane of brown fat cells also contains uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1), which provides a second route for protons to return to the matrix. When UCP1 is active, the energy from the oxidation of fatty acids, the main respiratory substrate in brown fat, is released as heat instead of being used to make ATP. (3) When the body is cold, the hypothalamus increases the frequency of impulses in sympathetic neurones that end in brown fat. These neurones release noradrenaline, which binds to receptors on the cell surface membrane of brown fat cells. This activates enzymes that hydrolyse the stored triglycerides, and the fatty acids released also activate UCP1. Repeated exposure to cold over several days increases the transcription of the gene coding for UCP1. (4) Until about 2009, adults were thought to have almost no brown fat. Then PET-CT scans using a radioactive glucose analogue, ¹⁸F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), revealed active brown fat in the neck and above the collar bones of many adults. In one study, 50 adult volunteers were each scanned twice: once after 2 hours at 16 °C and once after 2 hours at 27 °C. Active brown fat was detected in 33 of the volunteers after the cold exposure but in only 3 of them at 27 °C. (5) During the cold exposure, the oxygen consumption of the volunteers rose by 14% and their mean respiratory quotient (RQ) fell from 0.86 to 0.80. (6) Activating brown fat is being investigated as a treatment for obesity, but the idea has a dangerous history. In the 1930s, a chemical called 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) was sold as a slimming drug. DNP is a small molecule that picks up protons in the intermembrane space, diffuses across the inner mitochondrial membrane and releases the protons in the matrix. People taking DNP lost body mass rapidly, but several died of hyperthermia, with body temperatures above 43 °C. Unlike UCP1, DNP acts in the mitochondria of every tissue and its effect cannot be switched off by the body. State what is meant by the term respiratory substrate (paragraph 2). Explain how UCP1 causes the energy from the oxidation of fatty acids to be released as heat instead of being used to make ATP (paragraph 2). Explain how repeated exposure to cold could increase the transcription of the gene coding for UCP1 (paragraph 3). items.question: Use the information in the scientific article and your own knowledge to answer the questions that follow. Biological pacemakers: teaching heart cells to keep time (1) Each heartbeat begins in the sinoatrial node (SAN), a small group of specialised cardiac muscle cells in the wall of the right atrium. Unlike most other cells, SAN cells do not have a stable resting potential. Their membranes slowly depolarise until a threshold is reached and an action potential is produced. In an adult at rest this happens about 70 times a minute. A heart that has been removed from the body keeps beating, because cardiac muscle is myogenic. (2) In complete heart block, impulses from the SAN cannot pass through the atrioventricular node (AVN). The ventricles then beat at their own much slower rhythm, set by cells in the Purkyne fibres, often only 30 to 40 times a minute. Patients feel tired and breathless and may faint. The usual treatment is an electronic pacemaker: a battery-powered device under the skin connected by a wire to the right ventricle. More than a million are fitted worldwide each year, but the batteries must be replaced every 7 to 10 years, the wires can become infected, and the devices cannot speed up the heart during exercise in the way that a healthy SAN does. (3) Researchers have now made a 'biological pacemaker'. The gene coding for TBX18, a transcription factor that is active in the SAN of developing embryos, was inserted into a harmless virus. The virus was injected into a small area of the wall of the right ventricle of pigs with complete heart block. In the infected cells, TBX18 switched on genes for proteins found in SAN cells, including ion channels that allow the slow depolarisation, and switched off genes for proteins found in ordinary ventricular muscle cells. (4) Two days after the injection, the treated pigs had a mean heart rate of 78 beats per minute during the day, compared with 51 beats per minute in control pigs injected with the same virus carrying a gene for green fluorescent protein. path: Unit 5 Respiration, Internal Environment, Coordination and Gene Technology

B7.13 - (i) be able to calculate cardiac output (ii)
items.question: When a person has a heart transplant, the nerves that connected the heart to the brain are cut. These nerves do not regrow for several years, but the transplanted heart continues to beat. Scientists measured the heart rates of a group of heart transplant recipients and of a control group of people of similar age who had not had a transplant. Each person rested for 4 minutes, cycled at a constant moderate rate for 8 minutes and then rested again for 10 minutes. The graph shows the mean heart rate of each group. The cardiovascular control centre is found in the cerebellum cerebrum hypothalamus medulla oblongata The mean stroke volume of the control group at rest was 74 cm³. Calculate the mean cardiac output of the control group at rest. Give your answer in dm³ min⁻¹ to two significant figures. Compare the changes in the heart rates of the two groups during exercise and recovery. Using the information in the graph and your own knowledge, explain the differences between the heart rates of the two groups at rest, during exercise and during recovery.
items.ms: D — the cardiovascular control centre (and the ventilation centre) are in the medulla oblongata Resting heart rate read from the graph = 68 beats min⁻¹ and cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume (68 × 74 = 5032 cm³ min⁻¹) 5.0 dm³ min⁻¹ The heart rate of the control group rises rapidly / within 2–4 minutes of starting to cycle, whereas the heart rate of the transplant recipients rises slowly / steadily throughout the exercise The control group's heart rate levels off (at 122 beats min⁻¹) during exercise, whereas the transplant recipients' heart rate is still rising when exercise stops Both groups reach a similar maximum heart rate (about 122 and 120 beats min⁻¹) / the increase from rest is larger in the control group (54 compared with 24 beats min⁻¹) After exercise, the control group's heart rate falls immediately and rapidly, whereas the transplant recipients' heart rate keeps rising for about 2 minutes and then falls slowly At 22 minutes the control group's heart rate has returned to its resting value (68), whereas the transplant recipients' is still above their resting value (107 compared with 96) IC1 At rest, in the control group, impulses from the cardiovascular control centre pass along the vagus (parasympathetic) nerve to the SAN and slow it, so the resting heart rate is lower (68 beats min⁻¹) IC2 In the transplant recipients no impulses reach the SAN, so it depolarises at its own (faster) rate because cardiac muscle is myogenic (96 beats min⁻¹) IC3 In the control group, at the start of exercise, a rise in blood carbon dioxide / fall in pH is detected by chemoreceptors; more impulses pass from the cardiovascular control centre in the medulla oblongata along the sympathetic nerve to the SAN, so it depolarises more frequently; nerve impulses act quickly, so heart rate rises within minutes IC4 In the transplant recipients the rise in heart rate depends on adrenaline, released from the adrenal glands into the blood, binding to receptors on the SAN / cardiac muscle cells IC5 Adrenaline takes time to be secreted, to build up in the blood and to reach the heart, so the heart rate of the transplant recipients rises slowly and does not level off during exercise IC6 In recovery the control group's heart rate falls quickly because fewer impulses pass along the sympathetic nerve and more along the vagus nerve; in the transplant recipients adrenaline stays in the blood until it is broken down and there is no vagus nerve to slow the SAN, so heart rate falls slowly

items.question: A student used a spirometer to investigate the effect of exercise on breathing. The spirometer chamber was filled with oxygen and contained soda lime. items.question: Negative feedback keeps the sodium ion concentration of the blood plasma within narrow limits. Which of the following is an example of negative feedback? More sodium ion channels open as the membrane of an axon becomes depolarised A rise in body temperature increases the rate of metabolic reactions, which releases more heat The release of a hormone causes a response that increases the release of that hormone A decrease in the water potential of the blood causes more ADH to be released Plasma sodium ion concentration is normally kept within 3.0 % of 140 mmol dm⁻³. items.name: Homeostasis, dynamic equilibrium and thermoregulation; role of the hypothalamus
path: Unit 5 Respiration, Internal Environment, Coordination and Gene Technology
Topic 7 Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment
B7.17 - what is meant by the term homeostasis and its
items.question: Read the passage, then use the information in it and your own knowledge to answer the questions. Running hot 1 During a marathon, the rate of respiration in a runner's leg muscles rises more than ten-fold. Only about a quarter of the energy released is used for muscle contraction; the rest is released as heat. Yet in most runners, core body temperature rises by only 1–2 °C and then stays almost constant for the rest of the race. The body is far from resting, but it is in a state of dynamic equilibrium. 2 Thermoreceptors in the skin and in the hypothalamus detect the rise in temperature. The hypothalamus then brings about vasodilation in the skin and increases the secretion of sweat. Evaporation of 1 g of sweat removes about 2.4 kJ of heat. In humid air, much of the sweat drips off the skin without evaporating. 3 At one championship marathon, held at midnight to avoid the heat of the day, the air temperature was still 32 °C and the humidity 74%. Of the 68 runners who started, 28 did not finish. In hot conditions runners show 'cardiovascular drift'. In one runner, the heart rate after 20 minutes was 150 beats min⁻¹ and the stroke volume 120 cm³; after 90 minutes at the same pace, the heart rate was 172 beats min⁻¹ and the stroke volume 102 cm³. Meanwhile, more blood flowed to the skin and sweat was lost at up to 1.5 dm³ per hour, reducing the volume of the blood plasma. 4 Sweat is mainly water, so heavy sweating raises the solute concentration of the blood plasma. More antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is secreted and the volume of urine falls. However, runners who drink far more water than they lose can dilute their blood dangerously. 5 Athletes who train in the heat for 10 to 14 days become acclimatised. They start to sweat at a lower core temperature, their plasma volume increases by up to 10% and, at any given running speed, their heart rate is lower. 6 Heat also causes some proteins inside cells to unfold. A transcription factor called heat shock factor 1 (HSF1) is normally held in an inactive form in the cytoplasm. When the cell is heated, HSF1 is released, enters the nucleus and switches on the genes for heat shock proteins. These proteins bind to unfolded proteins and help them to fold correctly again. Acclimatised athletes have more heat shock proteins in their muscle cells. 7 If heat production continues to exceed heat loss, core temperature can rise above 40 °C, causing heat stroke. As the temperature rises, metabolic reactions speed up and release even more heat. Rapid cooling, for example in a bath of iced water, is the most effective treatment. Explain why the body of a marathon runner can be described as being in a state of dynamic equilibrium (paragraph 1). Explain how the hypothalamus brings about the responses described in paragraph 2, and how these responses reduce core body temperature. Calculate the percentage change in the cardiac output of the runner between 20 minutes and 90 minutes (paragraph 3). Explain why the runner's heart rate increased between 20 minutes and 90 minutes of running at the same pace (paragraph 3). Explain how the increase in the solute concentration of the blood plasma leads to a fall in the volume of urine produced (paragraph 4). Suggest how the changes described in paragraph 5 allow an acclimatised athlete to run at a given speed with a lower heart rate. Explain how heating muscle cells leads to the production of more heat shock proteins (paragraph 6). The rise in core temperature described in paragraph 7 is an example of dynamic equilibrium homeostasis negative feedback positive feedback
items.ms: Internal conditions (core temperature) are kept within narrow limits by homeostasis / negative feedback Although heat production is high and changing, the rate of heat loss is continually adjusted to match it / heat loss balances heat gain There are constant small fluctuations around a set point / the body is constantly responding to changes Impulses from the thermoreceptors / the rise in blood temperature are received by the thermoregulatory (heat loss) centre in the hypothalamus Impulses are sent along (sympathetic / motor) neurones to the effectors Smooth muscle in the walls of arterioles supplying the skin relaxes (vasodilation), so more blood flows through capillaries near the skin surface So more heat is lost from the blood by radiation (and convection) Sweat glands secrete more sweat; evaporation of water from the sweat uses (latent) heat from the skin As core temperature returns towards the set point, fewer impulses are sent (negative feedback) Cardiac output = 150 × 120 = 18 000 cm³ min⁻¹ and 172 × 102 = 17 544 cm³ min⁻¹ (17 544 − 18 000) ÷ 18 000 × 100 = −2.5 % (a decrease of 2.5 %) Lower plasma (blood) volume and more blood in the skin, so less blood returns to the heart and the stroke volume falls The fall in blood pressure is detected by baroreceptors / the change is detected by chemoreceptors Impulses to the cardiovascular control centre in the medulla oblongata More impulses along the sympathetic nerve to the SAN, so the SAN depolarises more frequently So cardiac output / oxygen delivery to the muscles is (almost) maintained Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the fall in the water potential of the blood Impulses to the (posterior) pituitary gland, which releases more ADH ADH binds to receptors on cells of the collecting duct / DCT, so more aquaporins are inserted into their membranes Walls more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood by osmosis Larger plasma (blood) volume, so more blood returns to the heart and the stroke volume is larger So the same cardiac output (and oxygen delivery) is achieved at a lower heart rate, because cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume Sweating starts sooner, so core temperature stays lower and less blood needs to be diverted to the skin HSF1 binds to the promoter (region) of the heat shock protein genes Allowing RNA polymerase to bind / stimulating transcription of the genes mRNA is produced and leaves the nucleus (through nuclear pores) mRNA is translated at ribosomes to make heat shock proteins D — the rise in temperature speeds up metabolism, which releases more heat and raises the temperature further: the change is amplified

items.question: People with type 2 diabetes have a high concentration of glucose in their blood. One drug used to treat type 2 diabetes binds to the sodium–glucose co-transporter proteins in the cells of the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT). The graph shows the rate of glucose loss in the urine at different plasma glucose concentrations, for people taking the drug and for people taking a placebo. Describe how glucose is reabsorbed from the filtrate in the PCT of a person who is not taking the drug. The rate at which glucose is filtered can be calculated using this formula. rate of filtration = glomerular filtration rate × plasma glucose concentration The glomerular filtration rate is 125 cm³ min⁻¹ and 1 mmol of glucose has a mass of 180 mg. items.question: Furosemide is a drug that inhibits the transport proteins that move sodium ions and chloride ions out of the filtrate in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Scientists gave rats either furosemide or a solution without the drug (control). They measured the solute concentration of the tissue fluid at different distances into the medulla, the rate of urine production and the solute concentration of the urine. The graph and the table show the results. items.question: Read the passage, then use the information in it and your own knowledge to answer the questions. Thin air and the oxygen switch 1 Many endurance athletes prepare for major competitions by living and training at high altitude for several weeks. At 2500 m above sea level, air has the same percentage of oxygen as at sea level, but the air pressure is about 25% lower, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood in the lungs. During their first few days at altitude, athletes find that their resting heart rate and ventilation rate are higher than usual. 2 After a few days, the kidneys release more of the hormone erythropoietin (EPO). EPO is a glycoprotein: a chain of 165 amino acids with four carbohydrate chains attached. It travels in the blood to the bone marrow, where it binds to receptors on the cell surface membranes of the cells that divide to form red blood cells. This activates a series of enzymes inside these cells. As a result, genes that stop the cells from dying and genes needed to make haemoglobin are switched on, and more red blood cells enter the blood. 3 How do kidney cells detect a shortage of oxygen? The answer, which led to a Nobel Prize in 2019, is a transcription factor called hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF). When oxygen is plentiful, an enzyme uses oxygen to add hydroxyl groups to HIF, which is then broken down within about five minutes. When oxygen is scarce, the enzyme cannot work, so HIF moves into the nucleus and binds to a specific base sequence close to the EPO gene. Transcription of the EPO gene can increase more than 100-fold. 4 As the number of red blood cells rises, more oxygen reaches the kidney cells and less EPO is secreted. In this way the haematocrit, the percentage of the blood volume made up of red blood cells, is normally kept between 40% and 50%. 5 People with chronic kidney disease often become anaemic because their kidneys make too little EPO. They can be treated with recombinant human EPO, made by cells from the ovaries of Chinese hamsters into which the human EPO gene has been inserted. The cells are grown in fermenters and secrete EPO with its carbohydrate chains attached. Newer drugs, taken as tablets, inhibit the enzyme that adds hydroxyl groups to HIF. 6 In one study, 12 runners lived at 2500 m for four weeks. Their mean total haemoglobin mass increased from 875 g to 931 g, and their maximum rate of oxygen uptake increased by 4%. 7 Some athletes have tried to gain the same advantage by injecting recombinant EPO, which is banned in sport. It can raise the haematocrit above 55%, making the blood more viscous. Athletes who inject EPO also secrete less EPO from their own kidneys. Explain why the resting heart rate and ventilation rate of the athletes are higher than usual during their first few days at altitude (paragraph 1). EPO does not enter the cells of the bone marrow. Explain how EPO causes genes to be switched on in these cells (paragraph 2). Which of the following describes HIF in a kidney cell when there is plenty of oxygen (paragraph 3)? HIF is hydroxylated and broken down, so transcription of the EPO gene is not increased HIF binds to the EPO gene and prevents RNA polymerase from binding HIF is made more slowly because the gene coding for HIF is switched off HIF enters the nucleus but cannot bind to DNA without oxygen Explain how a low oxygen concentration in the kidney leads to an increase in the concentration of EPO in the blood (paragraph 3). Suggest why recombinant human EPO is made using hamster cells rather than bacteria (paragraph 5). Suggest how the newer drugs described in paragraph 5 could treat anaemia in people with chronic kidney disease. Calculate the percentage increase in the mean total haemoglobin mass of the runners (paragraph 6). Explain why athletes who inject recombinant EPO secrete less EPO from their own kidneys (paragraphs 4 and 7).

medulla oblongata More impulses along the sympathetic nerve to the SAN, so the SAN depolarises more frequently More impulses to the intercostal muscles and diaphragm, so they contract more frequently So more oxygen is taken into the blood and delivered to the tissues per minute, compensating for the lower oxygen content of each volume of blood EPO is a large, water-soluble (glyco)protein, so it cannot diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer The enzymes activated inside the cell activate transcription factors (in the cytoplasm) The transcription factors move into the nucleus and bind to the promoter (region) of the genes So RNA polymerase can bind and the genes are transcribed to mRNA A — with plenty of oxygen the enzyme adds hydroxyl groups to HIF and the HIF is broken down, so it cannot act as a transcription factor for the EPO gene HIF acts as a transcription factor, binding to the promoter (region) of the EPO gene so that RNA polymerase can bind More transcription of the EPO gene, so more EPO mRNA is made The mRNA leaves the nucleus (through a nuclear pore) and is translated at ribosomes (on the rough endoplasmic reticulum) The polypeptide is modified in the Golgi apparatus (carbohydrate chains added) and packaged into vesicles EPO is secreted into the blood by exocytosis EPO needs carbohydrate chains attached after translation Bacteria have no Golgi apparatus / cannot add carbohydrate chains to proteins, whereas hamster cells are mammalian (eukaryotic) cells like human cells Without the carbohydrate chains, EPO might have the wrong shape / not bind to its receptor / be broken down quickly Hydroxyl groups are not added to HIF, so HIF is not broken down even when oxygen is present HIF binds near the EPO gene, so more EPO is transcribed and secreted (by the remaining kidney cells) So more red blood cells / haemoglobin are made (931 − 875) ÷ 875 × 100 6.4 % Injected EPO increases the number of red blood cells / the haematocrit So more oxygen is delivered to the kidney cells So HIF is hydroxylated and broken down, and transcription of the EPO gene decreases This is negative feedback: the response (more oxygen) removes the original stimulus (low oxygen)

items.question: The passage below is adapted from a scientific article about itch. Use the information in the passage and your own knowledge to answer the questions. Scratching the surface: the biology of itch (1) Itch is an unpleasant sensation that causes a desire to scratch. For many years itch was thought to be a mild form of pain, but scientists now know that it is detected by its own set of sensory neurones. The receptors for itch are the branched, free nerve endings of these neurones in the outer layer of the skin. Pain usually triggers a withdrawal reflex that moves the body away from the stimulus, whereas itch triggers scratching, which is directed towards the stimulus. (2) When a mosquito bites, cells in the skin release histamine. Histamine binds to receptor proteins in the membrane of the nerve endings of itch neurones. This opens cation channels called TRPV1. If the stimulus is large enough, action potentials pass along the neurone towards the spinal cord. Most itch neurones are unmyelinated C fibres, about 1 μm in diameter, that conduct impulses at about 0.5 m s⁻¹. In contrast, the neurones that detect touch are myelinated and conduct impulses at about 50 m s⁻¹. (3) The cell bodies of itch neurones lie in the dorsal root ganglia. Inside the spinal cord, itch impulses are passed to relay neurones that carry them towards the brain. Neurones in this pathway release glutamate and a second neurotransmitter, gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP). The relay neurones that carry itch impulses have receptors for GRP. In one study, scientists produced mice in which the GRP receptor gene had been knocked out (inactivated). When injected with chloroquine, a drug that causes itch without the release of histamine, these mice scratched 26 times in 30 minutes, compared with 198 times for normal mice. When histamine was injected instead, the two groups scratched a similar number of times. (4) Scratching stimulates touch and pain neurones in the skin. In the spinal cord, these neurones stimulate inhibitory relay neurones, which release an inhibitory neurotransmitter onto the relay neurones that carry itch impulses. Brain scans of volunteers using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) show that scratching reduces activity in regions linked with the unpleasant feeling of itch and increases activity in regions linked with reward. This may explain why scratching feels pleasant and is hard to stop. (5) Chronic itch, lasting more than six weeks, affects about one person in five at some time in their life, often because of the skin condition eczema. Scratching damages the skin, which then releases more itch-causing substances, so an itch–scratch cycle develops. Researchers used microarrays to compare gene activity in skin from people with eczema and from people with healthy skin. More than 300 genes were more active in the eczema skin, including genes coding for receptors on itch neurones. These receptors are now targets for new drugs. Explain why the free nerve endings of itch neurones are described as receptors (paragraph 1). Explain how the binding of histamine to its receptors can lead to an action potential in an itch neurone (paragraph 2). Paragraph 2 compares itch neurones with touch neurones. A mosquito bites a person's ankle. The distance from the ankle to the spinal cord is 1.1 m. Calculate the difference between the times taken for impulses in an itch neurone and in a touch neurone to travel from the ankle to the spinal cord. Explain why impulses travel more slowly in itch neurones than in touch neurones. Name the region of the spinal cord in which itch neurones synapse with relay neurones (paragraph 3). Explain what the results of the study described in paragraph 3 suggest about how itch caused by chloroquine and itch caused by histamine are transmitted in the spinal cord. Suggest how the inhibitory neurotransmitter released in the spinal cord during scratching could reduce the itch that is felt (paragraph 4). Describe how microarrays could be used to compare gene activity in skin from people with eczema and from people with healthy skin (paragraph 5).

depolarisation reaches threshold (about −55 mV), voltage-gated sodium ion channels open more sodium ions enter (positive feedback), so the inside becomes positive (about +40 mV), producing an action only occurs at the nodes of Ranvier so the impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction) in itch neurones (no myelin) the whole length of the axon membrane must be depolarised itch neurones have a small diameter (1 μm), so there is more resistance to the flow of ions along the axon grey matter chloroquine itch depends on GRP binding to GRP receptors, as mice without the receptors In the knee-jerk reflex, a sensory neurone from a stretch receptor in the thigh muscle synapses directly with a motor neurone in the spinal cord. There is no relay neurone. items.ms: C receptor (in the skin) stimulates the sensory neurone, which carries the impulse into the spinal cord through the dorsal root (ganglion) sensory neurone synapses with a relay neurone in the grey matter relay neurone synapses with a motor neurone (in the grey matter) motor neurone carries the impulse out of the spinal cord (through the ventral root) to the muscle (effector), where it forms a neuromuscular junction conduction times: 0.58 ÷ 72 = 8.1 ms and 0.60 ÷ 60 = 10.0 ms (total 18.1 ms) 20.4 − 18.1 = 2.3 ms the withdrawal reflex has a relay neurone, so impulses cross two synapses in the spinal cord rather than one transmission at each synapse takes time: calcium ion entry, exocytosis of neurotransmitter, diffusion across the cleft and binding to receptors diffusion of neurotransmitter across the cleft is slower than conduction of an action potential along an axon

items.question: Squid giant axons can be kept alive for several hours in sea water. A scientist added cyanide to the sea water around a squid giant axon. items.ms: D the sodium–potassium pump actively transports sodium ions out and potassium ions in (using ATP) more sodium ions are pumped out than potassium ions are pumped in (3 : 2) the membrane is more permeable to potassium ions (some K⁺ channels open) than to sodium ions (Na⁺ channels closed) potassium ions diffuse out (down their concentration gradient) so the inside of the axon is negative compared with the outside (288 − 400) ÷ 400 × 100 −28% / a decrease of 28% cyanide inhibits the electron transport chain / the final carrier (cytochrome oxidase), so oxygen cannot act as the final electron acceptor so oxidative phosphorylation stops and little ATP is made (only by glycolysis) the sodium–potassium pump cannot work / less active transport of Na⁺ out and K⁺ in potassium ions continue to diffuse out (and sodium ions leak in), so the concentration gradients run down so the inside becomes less negative / the resting potential rises from −70 to −53 mV

items.question: The graphs show the changes in the membrane potential of an axon and in the permeability of its membrane to sodium ions (Na⁺) and potassium ions (K⁺) after the axon was stimulated at 0.5 ms. At which time are most voltage-gated potassium ion channels open while most voltage-gated sodium ion channels are closed? 0.3 ms 1.2 ms 2.2 ms 4.8 ms The threshold potential of this axon is −55 mV. Calculate the mean rate of depolarisation between the threshold potential and the peak of the action potential. Give your answer in mV ms⁻¹. items.ms: C change in potential = 40 − (−55) = 95 mV and time = 1.5 − 1.0 = 0.5 ms 95 ÷ 0.5 = 190 mV ms⁻¹ IC1 0.5–1.0 ms: the stimulus opens some sodium ion channels; Na⁺ diffuse in, so the potential rises from −70 mV to the threshold (−55 mV at 1.0 ms) IC2 at threshold, more voltage-gated sodium ion channels open (positive feedback): permeability to Na⁺ rises steeply to a peak of about 100 a.u. at about 1.35 ms IC3 rapid influx of Na⁺ (down the electrochemical gradient) depolarises the membrane so the inside becomes positive, reaching +40 mV at 1.5 ms IC4 sodium ion channels then close, so permeability to Na⁺ falls back to its resting level by about 1.8 ms and Na⁺ stop entering IC5 voltage-gated potassium ion channels open more slowly: permeability to K⁺ peaks (about 40 a.u.) at about 2.3 ms; K⁺ diffuse out, so the membrane repolarises (back to −70 mV at about 2.9 ms) IC6 permeability to K⁺ stays above its resting level, so too many K⁺ leave and the membrane is hyperpolarised (−80 mV at 3.2 ms); then K⁺ channels close and the sodium–potassium pump / resting permeability restore −70 mV by 4.5 ms the peak would be lower / less positive / depolarisation would be slower because the sodium ion concentration gradient is smaller, so fewer Na⁺ diffuse in when the channels open threshold may not be reached, so no action potential is produced the axon is in its (absolute) refractory period voltage-gated sodium ion channels are closed / inactivated and cannot open again until the membrane has repolarised potassium ions are still leaving, so the inside is becoming more negative and threshold cannot be reached 1 ÷ 0.0025 = 400 (action potentials per second)

items.name: Central and peripheral nervous systems
path: Unit 5 Respiration, Internal Environment, Coordination and Gene Technology
Topic 8 Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
B8.10 - know that the mammalian nervous system consists of
items.question: The passage below is adapted from a scientific article about the vagus nerve. Use the information in the passage and your own knowledge to answer the questions. The wandering nerve (1) The mammalian nervous system has two parts. The central nervous system (CNS) is made up of the brain and spinal cord, and the peripheral nervous system (PNS) is made up of the nerves that connect the CNS with the rest of the body. The vagus nerve is the longest of the twelve pairs of cranial nerves. Its name comes from the Latin word for 'wandering', because it runs from the medulla oblongata, at the base of the brain, to the heart, lungs and much of the gut. About 80% of the neurones in the vagus nerve are sensory neurones; the rest are motor neurones, whose cell bodies lie in the medulla oblongata. (2) In 2000, researchers discovered that the vagus nerve also controls inflammation. When tissues are damaged or infected, white blood cells called macrophages release a protein called TNF. Sensory neurones in the vagus nerve detect TNF and send impulses to the brain. Impulses then return along vagus motor neurones and a nerve to the spleen, where acetylcholine is released close to macrophages. The acetylcholine binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the cell surface membrane of the macrophages, and this reduces the transcription of the TNF gene. The researchers called this pathway the 'inflammatory reflex'. (3) Electrical vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) has been used since 1997 to treat epilepsy that does not respond to drugs. A small stimulator is implanted under the skin of the chest and connected to an electrode wrapped around the left vagus nerve in the neck. The stimulator usually delivers pulses at 30 Hz for 30 seconds every 5 minutes. In one study of 120 patients, the mean number of seizures per month fell from 14.5 before the stimulator was fitted to 8.7 one year later. The right vagus nerve is not used because it carries more of the neurones that supply the sinoatrial node (SAN). (4) The most common side effects of VNS are a hoarse voice and coughing during each period of stimulation. A newer device stimulates a branch of the vagus nerve in the skin of the outer ear, so no surgery is needed. Brain scans using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) have shown that this stimulation activates the same regions of the brain stem as implanted devices. Small trials have also found that VNS lowers the concentration of TNF in the blood of people with rheumatoid arthritis, a disease in which the joints are inflamed. Explain why the vagus nerve is part of the peripheral nervous system, even though the cell bodies of its motor neurones are in the brain (paragraph 1). Give two differences between the functions of the sensory neurones and the motor neurones in the vagus nerve (paragraph 1). Suggest how the binding of acetylcholine to receptors in the cell surface membrane of macrophages could reduce the transcription of the TNF gene (paragraph 2). Explain why the inflammatory reflex is an example of negative feedback (paragraph 2). Suggest why nicotine could reduce the production of TNF by macrophages (paragraph 2). Calculate the percentage decrease in the mean number of seizures per month in the study described in paragraph 3. Explain why stimulating the right vagus nerve could cause a slow heart rate (paragraph 3). Suggest why patients develop a hoarse voice during each period of stimulation (paragraph 4). Explain how fMRI could be used to show which regions of the brain are activated when the skin of the outer ear is stimulated (paragraph 4).

the axons leave the CNS to reach the effectors sensory neurones carry impulses towards the CNS / medulla, whereas motor neurones carry impulses away from the CNS sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors (in the heart, lungs and gut), whereas motor neurones carry impulses to effectors (muscles or glands, e.g. the SAN or gut muscle) sensory neurones respond to stimuli (e.g. TNF, stretching of the lungs), whereas motor neurones bring about a response acetylcholine does not enter the macrophage; items.question: Scientists cut 10 mm segments from oat coleoptiles, just below the tip of each coleoptile. In a second experiment, segments were kept in different solutions for 2 hours. Buffers keep the pH of a solution constant. The table shows the results. Explain how these results support the hypothesis that IAA causes cell elongation by lowering the pH of the cell walls.
