items.question: Plants growing under a canopy of leaves receive light that has passed through other leaves. Chlorophyll absorbs most of the red light but transmits most of the far-red light, so the ratio of red light to far-red light (R : FR ratio) is much lower in shade than in full sunlight. Which of the following describes the phytochrome in the leaves of a plant growing in deep shade, compared with a plant growing in full sunlight? a higher proportion is in the Pfr form, because far-red light converts Pr to Pfr a higher proportion is in the Pfr form, because less red light reaches the leaves a higher proportion is in the Pr form, because far-red light converts Pfr to Pr a higher proportion is in the Pr form, because red light converts Pfr to Pr Scientists grew seedlings of one plant species under white light with different amounts of far-red light added. This gave different R : FR ratios while the intensity of the light used in photosynthesis stayed the same. After 14 days they measured the length of the third internode (the section of stem between the second and third leaves) and the concentration of active gibberellin (GA₁) in the stem. The graph shows the length of the third internode. The table shows the concentration of GA₁. An R : FR ratio of 1.2 is typical of full sunlight and a ratio of 0.2 is typical of shade under a canopy. Calculate the percentage increase in the length of the third internode when the R : FR ratio falls from 1.2 to 0.2. Suggest why the scientists kept the intensity of the light used in photosynthesis the same for all R : FR ratios. The scientists then grew more seedlings, some treated with paclobutrazol, a substance that inhibits the synthesis of gibberellins. Some of these seedlings were also sprayed with GA₁. The table shows the length of the third internode after 14 days. The lengths for seedlings given no treatment are shown on the graph. Deduce what these results show about how a low R : FR ratio increases internode length. Explain how a low R : FR ratio brings about the increase in internode length in these plants. Use the information in the graph, the tables and your own knowledge.
items.ms: C: far-red light (730 nm) is absorbed by Pfr and converts it to Pr, so with a low R : FR ratio more of the phytochrome is Pr. A and B have the conversion the wrong way round (less red light means less Pr is converted to Pfr); D gives the wrong wavelength: red light converts Pr to Pfr. lengths read from the graph as 14 mm and 40 mm (40 − 14) ÷ 14 × 100 = 186% light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis (so) affects the amount of sugars / ATP / materials available for growth of the stem so that any difference in internode length is caused only by the R : FR ratio / to make the results valid paclobutrazol reduces internode length much more at R : FR 0.2 (40 to 17 mm) than at 1.2 (14 to 9 mm), so the increase in shade depends on gibberellin (synthesis) adding GA₁ restores the length (39 mm compared with 40 mm), so paclobutrazol acts by stopping gibberellin synthesis / is not toxic with paclobutrazol, internodes are still longer at 0.2 than at 1.2 (17 and 9 mm), so some of the effect does not depend on gibberellin IC1 far-red light converts Pfr to Pr, so in a low R : FR ratio less phytochrome is in the active Pfr form IC2 Pfr normally inhibits / causes the breakdown of transcription factors that switch on genes for gibberellin synthesis; with less Pfr these transcription factors are active / the genes are transcribed IC3 data: GA₁ rises from 1.3 to 4.1 ng g⁻¹ as the R : FR ratio falls from 1.2 to 0.1, while internode length rises from 14 to 44 mm IC4 data: blocking gibberellin synthesis removes most of the increase at R : FR 0.2 (17 mm) and adding GA₁ restores it (39 mm), so the increase is caused by gibberellin IC5 gibberellin binds to a receptor and causes the breakdown of repressor proteins / activates transcription factors, so genes for stem growth are transcribed; mRNA is translated into proteins / enzymes IC6 cells in the internode elongate (and divide), so the stem grows taller, raising the leaves above the canopy to absorb more (red) light for photosynthesis
items.why: B8.11 is hot (10 of 17 sessions) with six-mark phytochrome answers in Jun2021, Oct2023 and Jan2026; the shade (R : FR) control of stem elongation through gibberellin has never been asked and links phytochrome to transcription.

items.question: Scientists investigated nervous and hormonal control of heart rate using a mammalian heart that was kept beating in a warm, oxygenated solution flowing through its blood vessels. items.question: A 58-year-old woman was taken to hospital with sudden weakness of her right arm and leg. Doctors suspected a stroke, which is caused either by a blood clot blocking an artery in the brain or by bleeding from a burst artery. A drug that dissolves blood clots improves recovery, but only if it is given within 4.5 hours of the start of the stroke. It must not be given if the stroke is caused by bleeding. The doctors first used a computed tomography (CT) scan. Which of the following describes how a CT scan produces an image? X-rays are passed through the head from many directions and a computer produces cross-sectional images radio waves are absorbed and emitted by hydrogen nuclei in a strong magnetic field, producing detailed images gamma rays produced by a radioactive tracer are detected, showing regions of high metabolic activity changes in the oxygen content of the blood are detected, showing regions of high neurone activity Suggest why a CT scan, rather than an MRI scan, was used as soon as the woman arrived at the hospital. The MRI scanner produced images of slices through the brain, each 5 mm thick. The table shows the area of damaged tissue in each slice. Calculate the volume of damaged tissue. Give your answer in cm³. During her recovery, fMRI scans were taken while the woman repeatedly opened and closed her right hand. The graph shows the volume of activated tissue in the motor cortex of each cerebral hemisphere, with mean values for healthy volunteers doing the same task. The table shows her grip strength in her right hand. Explain how fMRI shows which regions of the brain are active. Calculate the percentage increase in the volume of activated tissue in the left motor cortex between week 1 and week 12. items.name: Brain chemical imbalances: dopamine and Parkinson's, serotonin and depression
path: Unit 5 Respiration, Internal Environment, Coordination and Gene Technology
Topic 8 Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
B8.16 - how imbalances in certain naturally-occurring
items.question: Use the information from the scientific article below and your own knowledge to answer the questions that follow. Rethinking serotonin and depression (1) Depression is one of the commonest causes of ill health in the world, affecting about 280 million people. Its symptoms include persistent low mood, loss of pleasure, poor sleep and difficulty concentrating. For over 50 years, one explanation has been that depression results from an imbalance of neurotransmitters, especially low concentrations of serotonin at synapses in parts of the cerebral hemispheres that regulate mood. (2) Serotonin is made in neurones from the amino acid tryptophan. After it is released, its action is ended mainly by reuptake: a membrane protein called the serotonin transporter (SERT) moves serotonin back into the presynaptic neurone. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as fluoxetine, bind to SERT and block it. (3) SSRIs raise the concentration of serotonin in synapses within a few hours of the first dose, yet most patients feel no benefit for four to six weeks. One explanation involves autoreceptors: serotonin receptors in the membrane of the presynaptic neurone. When serotonin binds to them, the neurone releases less serotonin. During several weeks of SSRI treatment, the number of autoreceptors falls. A second explanation is that serotonin, acting through receptors on target neurones, increases the production of a protein called BDNF, which stimulates the growth of new dendrites and synapses. (4) In one trial, 240 adults with moderate depression were randomly allocated to receive an SSRI or a placebo tablet for 8 weeks. The trial was double-blind. The mean depression score (on a scale of 0 to 52, where a higher score means more severe depression) fell from 24 to 14 in the SSRI group and from 24 to 17 in the placebo group. (5) Positron emission tomography (PET) can measure how many SERT molecules an SSRI blocks. Volunteers are given a radioactive tracer that binds to SERT. In one study, a dose of 20 mg of an SSRI per day blocked about 80% of the SERT molecules in the brain; higher doses blocked only a few more. (6) About 95% of the body's serotonin is made by cells in the lining of the intestine, and gut bacteria affect how much is made. When gut bacteria from people with depression were transferred into mice raised without any gut bacteria, the mice showed depression-like behaviour. Microarray analysis showed that the activity of about 200 genes in the brains of these mice had changed. (7) New antidepressant drugs are being developed using the three-dimensional structures of SERT and of serotonin receptors. Computer programs test millions of virtual molecules to find those that fit the binding site of a chosen receptor, before any are made and tested on cells. Explain why serotonin is described as a neurotransmitter (paragraph 1). Explain how SSRIs increase the stimulation of postsynaptic neurones (paragraph 2). Suggest how the fall in the number of autoreceptors could explain the delay before SSRIs relieve depression (paragraph 3). Explain how serotonin could increase the production of BDNF by target neurones (paragraph 3). What was the percentage decrease in the mean depression score of the SSRI group (paragraph 4)? 29.2% 41.7% 58.3% 71.4% Explain why the trial included a placebo group and was double-blind (paragraph 4). Suggest how PET scans could have been used to show that a dose of 20 mg of an SSRI per day blocks about 80% of the SERT molecules (paragraph 5). Suggest how microarrays could have been used to show that the activity of genes in the brains of these mice had changed (paragraph 6). Suggest why knowing the three-dimensional structure of a serotonin receptor helps scientists to develop new drugs (paragraph 7).
items.ms: it is released from the presynaptic neurone (by exocytosis of vesicles) when an impulse arrives it diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane causing depolarisation / an action potential (or inhibition) in the postsynaptic neurone the SSRI binds to / blocks SERT in the presynaptic membrane so less serotonin is taken back into the presynaptic neurone serotonin stays in the synaptic cleft for longer / at a higher concentration so more serotonin binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, giving more depolarisation / more action potentials at first the extra serotonin binds to the autoreceptors, so the presynaptic neurone releases less serotonin, cancelling out the effect of the SSRI after several weeks there are fewer autoreceptors, so serotonin release is no longer reduced and the postsynaptic neurones are stimulated more serotonin binds to a receptor on the cell surface membrane of the target neurone this activates a transcription factor (through a second messenger / chain of reactions) the transcription factor binds to the promoter of the BDNF gene, allowing RNA polymerase to bind / transcription to start more BDNF mRNA is made and translated at ribosomes B: (24 − 14) ÷ 24 × 100 = 41.7%. A is the decrease for the placebo group (7 ÷ 24); C is the final score as a percentage of the starting score (14 ÷ 24); D divides by the final score (10 ÷ 14). the placebo group acts as a control: patients' expectations alone can reduce the score (17 in the placebo group), so the effect of the drug is the difference between the groups double-blind: neither the patients nor the doctors know who receives the drug, which removes bias in reporting or assessing the scores scan the same volunteers with the tracer before and after taking the SSRI the tracer binds to free SERT and emits positrons, producing gamma rays that are detected to form an image where the SSRI occupies SERT, less tracer binds, so less radiation is detected (from those brain regions) repeat with different doses and calculate the percentage fall in signal; find the dose giving an 80% fall extract mRNA from the (same region of the) brains of mice given bacteria from people with depression and from control mice make cDNA (using reverse transcriptase) labelled with fluorescent tags / dyes of different colours add to a microarray containing DNA probes for many genes, so the cDNA binds to complementary probes compare the fluorescence of each spot / use bioinformatics to identify genes with different activity molecules can be designed / selected with a shape complementary to the binding site, so that they bind specifically to that receptor

items.name: Producing drugs from genetically modified organisms
path: Unit 5 Respiration, Internal Environment, Coordination and Gene Technology

B8.17 - how drugs can be produced using genetically m
items.question: Use the information from the scientific article below and your own knowledge to answer the questions that follow. Medicines from carrot cells (1) Gaucher disease is an inherited condition caused by a recessive allele of the gene for the enzyme glucocerebrosidase (GCD). Without functional GCD, a lipid builds up inside macrophages, and the enlarged macrophages damage the spleen, liver and bone marrow. Patients can be treated by an infusion of GCD into the blood every two weeks. (2) The first GCD used for treatment was extracted from human placentas collected after birth; treating one patient for a year needed about 20 000 placentas. Since the 1990s, GCD has been made by genetically modified hamster cells grown in large stainless-steel bioreactors. In 2009, a virus contaminated one of these bioreactors and production stopped for several months, leaving many patients without treatment. (3) In 2012, GCD made by genetically modified carrot cells became the first medicine from plant cells approved for use in humans. A DNA copy of the human GCD gene, joined to a promoter that is active in carrot cells, was inserted into a plasmid of the bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens. The plasmid also carried a gene giving resistance to an antibiotic. The bacteria were used to infect carrot cells growing in culture, and the carrot cells were then grown on a medium containing the antibiotic. (4) The modified carrot cells are grown in disposable plastic bags, each holding up to 400 dm³ of a simple nutrient medium. Viruses that infect mammals cannot grow in plant cells. After about a week the cells are harvested, and the GCD is extracted and purified. (5) To work, GCD must be taken up by macrophages. This depends on chains of sugars attached to the enzyme that end in the sugar mannose, which binds to mannose receptors on macrophages. GCD made by hamster cells has to be treated with three further enzymes to expose the mannose. The carrot cells add mannose-ending sugar chains themselves. (6) In a trial, 31 adults with Gaucher disease were given the carrot-cell GCD for 9 months. Their mean spleen volume fell from 2300 cm³ to 1690 cm³. (7) Some companies now want to grow whole genetically modified plants, such as tobacco or lettuce, in open fields to make medicines more cheaply. Others are concerned about the effects on the environment and on the human food supply. Suggest two advantages of producing GCD using genetically modified cells rather than extracting it from human placentas (paragraphs 1 and 2). Which of the following describes a plasmid (paragraph 3)? a small circular molecule of double-stranded DNA, separate from the bacterial chromosome a small circular molecule of single-stranded RNA found in viruses the main circular chromosome of a bacterial cell a short length of DNA with a sticky end at each end Describe how restriction endonucleases and DNA ligase would be used to insert the GCD gene into the plasmid (paragraph 3). Explain why the GCD gene was joined to a promoter that is active in carrot cells (paragraph 3). Explain how the method in paragraph 3 produces a culture in which every carrot cell contains the human GCD gene. Suggest why GCD that can be taken up by macrophages could not be produced by genetically modified bacteria (paragraphs 4 and 5). Calculate the percentage decrease in mean spleen volume in the trial (paragraph 6). Give your answer to three significant figures. Give two reasons why the results of this trial do not show that carrot-cell GCD is as effective as hamster-cell GCD (paragraph 6). Discuss the risks and benefits of growing genetically modified plants that produce medicines in open fields (paragraph 7).
items.ms: large quantities can be made / supply is not limited by the number of placentas no risk of transmitting pathogens / viruses from human tissue the product is consistent in purity / activity no ethical issues about using human tissue / consent of donors A: plasmids are small rings of double-stranded DNA in bacteria, separate from the main chromosome. B describes no plasmid (plasmids are DNA); C is the bacterial chromosome; D describes a cut fragment, not a plasmid. the same restriction endonuclease cuts the DNA on either side of the GCD gene and cuts the plasmid producing complementary sticky ends the sticky ends of the gene and plasmid join by complementary base pairing / hydrogen bonds DNA ligase forms phosphodiester bonds (in the sugar–phosphate backbone), producing recombinant DNA RNA polymerase (and transcription factors) bind to the promoter to start transcription carrot transcription factors / RNA polymerase may not recognise the human promoter so the GCD gene is transcribed into mRNA and translated into GCD in the carrot cells Agrobacterium infects the carrot cells and transfers (part of) the recombinant plasmid DNA into them the DNA is incorporated into the carrot cell's chromosomes / DNA only some carrot cells take up the DNA the antibiotic resistance gene is on the same DNA, so only carrot cells containing the GCD gene survive on the antibiotic medium these cells divide by mitosis, giving a culture of genetically identical cells all containing the gene bacteria / prokaryotes have no Golgi apparatus / endoplasmic reticulum so they cannot add sugar chains to the protein / cannot glycosylate it so the GCD would have no mannose and would not bind to the mannose receptors on macrophages (2300 − 1690) ÷ 2300 × 100 26.5% no group of patients was given hamster-cell GCD for comparison small sample of 31 patients only 9 months / long-term effects not measured no measure of variation / statistical test only spleen volume was measured, not the liver or bones benefit: cheaper / large-scale production, using sunlight energy and no bioreactors benefit: no risk of contamination by viruses that infect mammals / medicines more available in poorer countries risk: pollen may transfer the gene to wild relatives or non-GM crops risk: the medicine could enter the human food chain / be eaten by animals or insects, with unknown effects / allergic reactions risk: the antibiotic resistance gene could be transferred to soil bacteria
items.why: Every WBI15 paper ends with a 20-mark article; GM drug production (B8.17–B8.19) was the article in Jan2021, Jun2024 and Jan2026, but a plant-cell culture making a human enzyme, with Agrobacterium and glycosylation, has not been used.

items.name: Recombinant DNA: restriction endonucleases and DNA ligase
path: Unit 5 Respiration, Internal Environment, Coordination and Gene Technology
Topic 8 Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
B8.18 - how recombinant DNA can be produced, includin
items.question: Restriction endonucleases are enzymes from bacteria. The table shows the recognition sequences of four restriction endonucleases and where each one cuts (↓). Each enzyme cuts both strands of the DNA in the same way. Which two enzymes produce DNA fragments with sticky ends that could be joined to each other? BamHI and EcoRI EcoRI and SmaI BamHI and Sau3AI SmaI and Sau3AI SmaI produces DNA fragments with blunt ends. Suggest why fragments with blunt ends are joined into plasmids less often than fragments with sticky ends. The DNA of a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria) contains 48 500 base pairs. If the four bases were arranged in a random order and were equally common, a particular sequence of n bases would be expected to occur once in every 4ⁿ base pairs. Calculate the number of times the BamHI recognition sequence would be expected to occur in this DNA. Explain why Sau3AI would cut this DNA into many more fragments than BamHI. In fact, BamHI cuts this DNA at only 5 sites. Suggest why this is different from your answer to (c)(i). A gene cut with Sau3AI was inserted into a plasmid cut with BamHI. One strand of the DNA at one of the joins had the sequence 5′-ATGGATCTAG-3′ Explain whether BamHI could cut the recombinant DNA at this join.
items.ms: C: BamHI (G↓GATCC) and Sau3AI (↓GATC) both leave the single-stranded sequence GATC, so their sticky ends are complementary. A: BamHI leaves GATC but EcoRI leaves AATT. B and D: SmaI cuts straight across, giving blunt ends with no sticky ends. blunt ends have no unpaired bases / no complementary single-stranded sequences so no hydrogen bonds form to hold the fragment and the plasmid together so DNA ligase can only join them if the ends happen to meet / fewer phosphodiester bonds are formed 4⁶ = 4096 (base pairs) 48 500 ÷ 4096 = 11.8, so about 12 its recognition sequence is only 4 bases long, so it is expected about once every 256 base pairs / it occurs more often by chance the bases are not in a random order / are not equally common (e.g. the proportion of G and C is not 50%) because the sequence codes for genes no: the sequence at the join is GGATCT, not the BamHI recognition sequence GGATCC the enzyme's active site is complementary to / binds only to GGATCC, so no enzyme–substrate complex forms
items.why: B8.18 exam items are mostly recall of 'cut with the same enzyme, join with ligase'; the 2023 MCQs (Oct2023 Q1a) show recognition and bonding detail is examinable, and compatible sticky ends and the frequency of recognition sequences have never been asked.

items.name: Recombinant DNA: restriction endonucleases and DNA ligase
path: Unit 5 Respiration, Internal Environment, Coordination and Gene Technology
Topic 8 Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
B8.18 - how recombinant DNA can be produced, includin
items.question: Chymosin is an enzyme used to make cheese. It was once extracted only from the stomachs of young calves, but most chymosin is now made by genetically modified microorganisms. To make the recombinant DNA, scientists first extracted chymosin mRNA from cells in the stomach lining of calves and used it to make DNA. Which enzyme is used to make DNA from mRNA? DNA ligase DNA polymerase restriction endonuclease reverse transcriptase Suggest one reason why the scientists made the DNA from mRNA from stomach lining cells rather than cutting the gene out of calf DNA. The DNA made from the mRNA was inserted into a longer DNA molecule. The diagram shows this DNA molecule and the plasmid used. The letters show where three restriction endonucleases, E, H and P, cut. Enzyme H does not cut the plasmid. The plasmid contains a gene for resistance to the antibiotic ampicillin (ampR). Explain which enzyme should be used to cut out the chymosin DNA and to cut the plasmid. Calculate the length of the recombinant plasmid. Describe how the chymosin DNA and the plasmid are joined to form recombinant DNA. The plasmids were mixed with bacteria, and the bacteria were grown on agar containing ampicillin. Some of the colonies that grew did not produce chymosin. Suggest why.
items.ms: D: reverse transcriptase uses an RNA template to make complementary DNA (cDNA). DNA ligase joins DNA fragments; DNA polymerase copies a DNA template; restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific base sequences. these cells are producing chymosin, so they contain many copies of chymosin mRNA (but only two copies of the gene) / DNA made from mRNA has no introns, so the microorganism can make a functional protein / the gene does not have to be found among all the DNA in the genome E, because it cuts on both sides of the chymosin DNA without cutting within it H cuts within the chymosin DNA (and does not cut the plasmid) P cuts within the ampR gene, so the marker gene would not work / bacteria with the plasmid could not be selected fragment = 4.2 − 0.8 = 3.4 kbp 3.4 + 4.4 = 7.8 kbp both are cut with the same restriction endonuclease, so they have complementary sticky ends the sticky ends are mixed and pair by complementary base pairing / hydrogen bonds form between the bases DNA ligase joins the sugar–phosphate backbones by forming phosphodiester bonds the sticky ends of some plasmids joined to each other without the chymosin DNA these plasmids still contain the ampR gene, so the bacteria survive on ampicillin the chymosin DNA may be inserted the wrong way round / not next to a promoter, so it is not transcribed
items.why: B8.18 is warm (10 of 17 sessions) and is usually a 'describe how' within a GM question (Oct2023 Q5b, Jan2025 Q5c); choosing an enzyme from a restriction map and calculating the size of a recombinant plasmid has not been asked.

items.name: Inserting recombinant DNA into cells
path: Unit 5 Respiration, Internal Environment, Coordination and Gene Technology
Topic 8 Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
B8.19 - how recombinant DNA can be inserted into othe
items.question: Scientists compared methods of inserting a plasmid into cells. The plasmid contained a gene for a fluorescent protein and a gene for resistance to the antibiotic ampicillin. Which method would be used to insert recombinant DNA into a fertilised egg cell of a goat? heat shock in calcium chloride solution microinjection into the nucleus infection with Agrobacterium tumefaciens cutting with a restriction endonuclease In one investigation, 0.25 μg of plasmid DNA was added to 0.1 cm³ of E. coli bacteria, which were then given a heat shock. Nutrient broth was added to give 1.0 cm³ of culture. Then 0.1 cm³ of this culture was spread on agar containing ampicillin. After incubation, 184 colonies grew. Calculate the transformation efficiency (the number of transformed bacteria per μg of plasmid DNA). Give your answer in standard form. Explain why the bacteria were spread on agar containing ampicillin. Electroporation is another way of inserting plasmids into cells. A short electric pulse is passed through a suspension of cells mixed with plasmid DNA. The graphs show the effect of the electric field strength on the percentage of cells that survive and on the number of transformed cells. Explain the effect of electric field strength on the number of transformed cells. Calculate how many times greater the highest transformation efficiency by electroporation is than the transformation efficiency by heat shock in (b).
items.ms: B: the DNA is injected through a fine needle directly into the nucleus of the zygote. A is used for bacteria; C infects plant cells; D cuts DNA but does not insert it into a cell. 184 × 10 = 1840 transformed bacteria in the culture 1840 ÷ 0.25 = 7.36 × 10³ per μg only a small proportion of bacteria take up the plasmid the plasmid carries the ampicillin resistance (marker) gene, so only bacteria that have taken up the plasmid survive / form colonies so each colony comes from a transformed bacterium and can be counted / selected the electric pulse makes temporary pores in the cell surface membrane / phospholipid bilayer as the field strength increases up to 12.5 kV cm⁻¹, more / larger pores form, so more plasmid DNA enters the cells above 12.5 kV cm⁻¹ the number falls because more cells are killed (survival falls from 40% to 4%) because the membrane is damaged too much / cannot reseal 6.2 × 10⁸ ÷ 7360 = 8.4 × 10⁴
items.why: B8.19 came up in 9 of 17 sessions, almost always as one mark point ('method of putting the vector in'); a question on how efficiently DNA enters cells, with an electroporation graph and a standard-form calculation, has not been asked.

items.name: Microarrays: identifying active genes
path: Unit 5 Respiration, Internal Environment, Coordination and Gene Technology
Topic 8 Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
B8.20 - how microarrays can be used to identify activ
items.question: Scientists used a microarray to investigate how 12 weeks of endurance training changes the activity of genes in human thigh muscle. The diagram shows their method. Explain why the scientists extracted mRNA rather than DNA from the muscle samples. The table shows the green and red fluorescence of the spots for six genes. A spot gives out red light, green light or a mixture of both. Equal red and green light appears yellow. Which colour would the spot for gene T appear? yellow green red no colour Calculate the percentage change in the activity of gene S after training. Explain how the changes in the activity of genes P, Q, R and S make the muscle better suited to endurance exercise. Suggest why the fluorescence for gene U is very low in both samples. A full microarray contains probes for about 20 000 genes. Explain why bioinformatics is needed to analyse the results.
items.ms: all cells / both samples contain the same genes in their DNA, whether the genes are active or not mRNA is only made from genes that are being transcribed / active the amount of mRNA shows how active each gene is A: gene T (actin) has almost equal green and red fluorescence (2400 and 2380), so the spot is yellow: the gene is equally active before and after training. B would mean more activity before training, C more after training, D no activity. (370 − 860) ÷ 860 × 100 −57% gene P: more electron transport chain proteins / more mitochondria, so more ATP from aerobic respiration (oxidative phosphorylation) gene Q: more myoglobin, which stores oxygen in the muscle / releases oxygen when the partial pressure is low gene R: more capillaries, so more oxygen and glucose delivered / more carbon dioxide removed gene S: less fast-twitch myosin, so the fibres become more like slow-twitch fibres so less anaerobic respiration / less lactate, and the muscle fatigues less the rhodopsin gene is not transcribed / active in muscle cells (it is only expressed in rod cells) there is a very large amount of data computer software / algorithms are used to compare the red and green fluorescence of every spot and identify genes whose activity changed (significantly) databases are used to identify the genes / their functions from the probe sequences
items.why: Microarrays came up in 6 sessions, always as 'describe how' (Oct2022 Q8b, Jan2024 Q5a); interpreting two-colour microarray data with a percentage change has never been asked, and the muscle adaptations link it to B7.10.

items.name: Bioinformatics
path: Unit 5 Respiration, Internal Environment, Coordination and Gene Technology

B8.21 - what is meant by the term bioinformatics
items.question: Cytochrome c is a protein in the electron transport chain of all eukaryotes. The table shows part of the amino acid sequence of cytochrome c in humans and in two other species, P and Q. Each letter represents one amino acid. Explain what is meant by the term bioinformatics. Calculate the percentage of amino acids in this part of the sequence of species Q that are the same as in humans. The DNA of a newly discovered species of fungus has been sequenced. Suggest how bioinformatics could be used to find out whether one of its genes codes for cytochrome c.
items.ms: the use of computers / software / algorithms / databases to store, organise and analyse (large amounts of) biological data, e.g. DNA base sequences or amino acid sequences 13 out of 25 are the same 52% compare the base sequence of the gene / the amino acid sequence it codes for with sequences in a database using a computer program to search for and align similar sequences a close match / high similarity to cytochrome c sequences of other species shows it is the cytochrome c gene
items.why: Bioinformatics has appeared in 6 sessions only as a mark point inside microarray or genome questions (Jan2022 Q8c homology, Jun2024 Q8a); the spec asks students to 'understand what is meant by' the term, which has never been asked on its own.

items.name: Risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms
path: Unit 5 Respiration, Internal Environment, Coordination and Gene Technology
Topic 8 Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
B8.22 - the risks and benefits associated with the us
items.question: Bt cotton is a genetically modified cotton plant containing a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. The gene codes for a protein (Bt toxin) that kills bollworm caterpillars, a major pest of cotton, when they eat the plant. Bt toxin binds to receptors found in the gut of these insects but not in mammals. The graphs show the percentage of the cotton-growing area in one country planted with Bt cotton, and the mass of insecticide used per hectare of cotton, from 2002 to 2014. The table shows the mean cotton yield. Calculate the percentage decrease in the mass of insecticide used per hectare of cotton between 2002 and 2010. Suggest one reason why the mass of insecticide used increased after 2010. Discuss the risks and benefits of growing Bt cotton. Use the information in the graphs and the table and your own knowledge.
items.ms: values read as 1.24 and 0.36 kg ha⁻¹ (1.24 − 0.36) ÷ 1.24 × 100 = 71% bollworms became resistant to Bt toxin (by natural selection) / other pests that are not killed by Bt toxin increased IC1 benefit: as Bt cotton rose from 1% to 76% of the area (2002 to 2008), mean yield rose from 302 to 506 kg ha⁻¹ because fewer plants are damaged by bollworms IC2 benefit: insecticide use fell by about 71% (to 0.36 kg ha⁻¹ in 2010), so lower costs for farmers and less harm to farm workers' health IC3 benefit: Bt toxin only affects insects with the receptors, so fewer non-target insects (pollinators, predators of pests) are killed than by sprayed insecticides / less pollution of water IC4 risk: after 2010 insecticide use rose to 0.56 kg ha⁻¹ and yield fell to 461 kg ha⁻¹, suggesting resistant bollworms (superpests) or secondary pests IC5 risk: pollen may transfer the Bt gene to wild relatives / non-GM cotton; Bt toxin could harm non-target insects that feed on the crop IC6 risk: farmers must buy expensive seed each year / monoculture reduces biodiversity IC7 the data show a correlation only: yield may also have changed because of weather, irrigation or fertilisers; data are from one country and have no error bars
items.why: GM risks and benefits came up in 4 sessions with 6-mark answers in Oct2022 and Oct2024; the ER notes benefits are tested less often than risks, and the rise of resistant pests after a Bt crop is adopted has not been asked with data.
